**Surah 74: al-Muddaththir**

Meccan (*makkiyyah*), according to Ibn 'Atiyyah, by scholarly consensus (*ijma'*). In *al-Tahrir*, Muqatil said that it is Meccan except for one verse, which is ﴿And We have not made their number except as a trial﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31], and so on. It will come, God willing, that there is an indication that His saying ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] is Medinan, with what that entails. Its verse count is fifty-six according to the Iraqi and the first Medinan counts, and fifty-five according to the Syrian and the last Medinan counts, as detailed in its proper place. It is linked to the surah before it by the opening with the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the beginnings of both are, according to the well-known view, revealed concerning a single event. The former began with the command to stand in prayer at night, which is a special worship, and this one begins with the command to warn, which contains a great deal of benefit for others.

Umayyah al-Azdi related from Jabir ibn Zayd, one of the scholars of the Successors (*tabi'un*) in the Qur'an, that al-Muddaththir was revealed immediately after al-Muzzammil. Ibn al-Durays also related from Ibn 'Abbas, and they regarded this as one of the reasons for placing it after it. The apparent meaning is that this view is weak.

For Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and a group [of others] narrated, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: "I asked Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman about the first thing of the Qur'an to be revealed, and he said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾. I said: 'They say it is ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1].' Abu Salamah said: 'I asked Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah about that, and I said to him what you have said, and Jabir said: "I will not tell you except what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) told us. He said: 'I stayed in seclusion in Hira'. When I had completed my seclusion, I came down, and I was called. I looked to my right and saw nothing; I looked to my left and saw nothing; I looked behind me and saw nothing. I raised my head and saw the angel who had come to me at Hira', sitting on a chair between heaven and earth. I was seized with terror from him, so I returned and said: 'Cover me! Cover me!' They covered me, and then there was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, ﴿Arise and warn﴾, ﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾.'"

In another narration: "I came to my family and said: 'Wrap me! Wrap me! Wrap me!' and God the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, up to His saying ﴿and abandon﴾."

The story is one story. If ﴿O you who are enwrapped﴾ had been the one revealed earlier, he would have mentioned it. Indeed, the apparent meaning of this report requires that ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed before ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾. However, what is transmitted in the two Sahihs and other works from 'A'ishah is that the latter was the first thing of the Qur'an to be revealed, and this is the view which most of the Community adopted, to the extent that some said it is the sound view. Because both reports are sound, they needed to answer. Al-Suyuti, in *al-Itqan*, transmitted five answers:

First: The question in the hadith of Jabir was about the revelation of a complete surah, so he explained that the surah of al-Muddaththir was revealed in its entirety before the completion of the surah "Read", since the first of it to be revealed was its beginning.

Second: Jabir's meaning of "first" is a first specific to the period after the pause in revelation (*fatrat al-wahy*), not an absolute first.

Third: The intended meaning is a first specific to the command to warn. Some expressed this by saying: the first thing revealed for prophethood was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, and the first thing revealed for messengerhood was ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾.

Fourth: The intended meaning is the first revealed with a prior cause, namely the wrapping that arose from terror. As for "Read", it was revealed at the outset without any prior cause.

Fifth: Jabir derived this by his own reasoning (*ijtihad*), and it is not from his own narration, so what 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) related takes precedence over it. Then he said: "The best of these answers are the first and the last." Ends. There is scrutiny in this, so consider it carefully and do not be heedless.

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾. Its original form is *al-mutadaththir*, which was assimilated (*udghima*, i.e. the two identical letters merged). It is in its original form in the reading of Ubayy: *man tadaththara*. It means he put on the *ditharr* (with a kasra on the dal), which is the garment above the shirt that is next to the body, and it is called *shi'ar* (undergarment) because it is in contact with the skin and the hair. From it comes his saying (ﷺ): "The Ansar are the undergarment, and the people are the outer garment."

The root, as is said, revolves around the meaning of covering in a comprehensive manner, as if the *ditharr* is a covering that is all-encompassing and hidden. The Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed with a name derived from his state at the time, as a means of intimacy and gentle affection, just as you have heard in ﴿O you who are wrapped in garments﴾. His wrapping himself (ﷺ) was for the reason you have just heard.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a weak chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah prepared a meal for Quraysh. When they had eaten, he said: "What do you say about this man?" They disagreed, then their opinion united on the view that he is a sorcerer whose magic is transmitted. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he grieved, covered his head, and wrapped himself, as a grieving person does. So God the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, up to His saying ﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾.

It is also said that what is meant by *al-Muddaththir* is the one wrapped in prophethood and the perfections of the soul, in the sense of one adorned with them and decorated by their effects. It is also said that *al-Muddaththir* is used and what is meant is the one absent from view, by way of metaphor and comparison, so it is an address to him by what he was in the cave of Hira'. It is also said: the apparent meaning is that by *al-Muddaththir*, and likewise by *al-Muzzammil*, is meant an allusion to the one at rest and free, because he was at the beginning of the mission. So it is as if it was said to him (ﷺ): "The time of rest has passed, and the hardships of obligations and the guidance of people have come to you, and you know that." This does not contradict the intended literal meaning, and the matter of gentle address remains as it is.

Some of the masters said: that is, O you who conceal the Muhammadan reality (*al-haqiqah al-muhammadiyyah*) under the garment of the human form, or O you who are hidden from the gaze of creation, so none knows you in reality except God the Exalted, and other such expressions. All of them are an indication of what they said about the Muhammadan reality, that it is the reality of realities, whose essence none of the creatures can grasp. On its tongue one who said said:

"Though I am a son of Adam in form,
in him there is a meaning that bears witness to my fatherhood."

And that it is the first determination (*al-ta'ayyun al-awwal*) and the keeper of the sealed secret; and that it, and that it... to matters at which the intellect cannot reach its end.

"He wearied the creatures; they could not grasp its meaning,
and none sees it, near or far, without being bewildered.

Like the sun which appears to the eyes from afar
small, and makes the gaze weary from its brilliance.

And how can one grasp its reality in this world
when a people asleep consoled themselves about it with dreams?

So the furthest extent of knowledge of it is that he is a human,
and that he is the best of all God's creation."

'Ikrimah read *al-mudathir* with a light dal and a heavy, kasra-marked tha', in the pattern of the active participle. And from him also: *al-mudaththar* with light and heavy forms, in the pattern of the passive participle, from *daththarahu*. And it is said: "*daththarta hadha al-amr*" and "*'usiba bika*", meaning: it was tied. The meaning is that he is the one relied upon; great matters are entrusted to him, and the affairs of their loosening and binding are tied to him. So it is as if it was said: O you on whom the affairs of people depend, for he is their means to God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿قُمْ﴾ means: rise from your bed, or rise with the resolve and determination of one who is set on something. Abu Hayyan took it, in this sense, to be one of the inceptive verbs (af'al al-shuruu, verbs indicating the beginning of an action), as in their saying "Zayd began (qama) to do such-and-such," and in the line of poetry: "Why does this base fellow begin (qama) to abuse me?" He also placed it in this sense among the sisters of kada (verbs of approximation, such as "he nearly did"). It has been objected that this usage is far from clear here, because it is not a familiar usage, the imperative of such a verb is not well attested, and it requires supplying a predicate for it. All of this is far-fetched. ﴿فَأنْذِرْ﴾ means: carry out the warning, or initiate it. Therefore no specific person is intended as the one warned. It has also been said that the object is to be understood as specific, meaning: "Warn your nearest kinsfolk," since this suits the actual beginning of the call. And it has been said that the object is to be understood as general, meaning: "Warn all of mankind," in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good news and a warner to all mankind﴾ [Saba': 28]. He did not say here "and give good news" (wa-bashshir), because this was at the beginning of prophethood, and warning was then the predominant mode, or because it is a sufficiency, since warning necessarily entails good news. In this command, after that call, there is an indication, according to some of the masters (al-sadah), of the station of manifestation (al-jilwah) after seclusion (al-khalwah). They said: the indication also refers to both of these in the hadith: "I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known," etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 3:

﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾. Single out your Lord for glorification, which means describing Him, exalted is He, with greatness and magnificence, both in belief and in speech.

It is narrated that when this (verse) was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Allahu akbar (Allah is greater)," and Khadijah glorified (Allah), rejoiced, and became certain that it was revelation (wahy, divine inspiration).

That is because Satan does not command such a thing, and a command addressed to him (ﷺ) is free from the need for inference. (The commentator) also permitted that it be understood as referring to the takbir (the opening proclamation "Allahu akbar") of the prayer.

Ibn Mardawayh has indeed reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We said, 'O Messenger of Allah, how should we say (it) when we enter the prayer?' Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed ﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to open the prayer with the takbir."

You know that this verse was revealed at a time when there was no prayer at all. So this report, if it is authentic, must be interpreted (ta'wil). The fa' (al-fa', "then") here and in what follows conveys the meaning of a conditional (shart, condition), so it is as if it were said: "Whatever (ma) happens, namely, whatever occurs, do not leave off His glorification, mighty and majestic is He." The fa' is then a response particle (fa' jaza'iyyah), and according to what has been said it is "displaced" (muzahlaqah), so the operation of what follows it does not harm what precedes it. It has also been said that it entered their speech by way of an imagined conditional, and since it was not in the response to a realized condition, it was in reality superfluous, so there was no obstacle to placing the object of what follows it before it for this reason.

Furthermore, the mention of this sentence after the earlier command, placed before the other sentences, indicates heightened concern with the matter of glorifying (Allah), and it hints, as has been said, that the primary purpose of the command to rise is that he should glorify his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, and declare Him free of association (shirk), for the first obligation is knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and then declaring Him free of what is unfitting to His sublime Presence. The speech on this is in the manner of the proverb: "It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour (iyyaka a'ni wa-isma'i ya jarah)." It may also be said that perhaps the mention of this sentence in this way is a hastening to encourage him, upon him be prayer and peace, to warn (the people) and to be unconcerned with anything other than Him, mighty and majestic is He, since it contains an indication that the forelocks of all creatures are in His hand, exalted is He, and that everything other than Him is subdued beneath His greatness and magnificence, exalted is He. Therefore one should not fear (illa, "except") Him, nor should one hope (illa, "except") in anything other than Him. So it is as if it were said: "Arise and warn, and single out your Lord for glorification, so that nothing turns you away from warning. So reflect."

And your garments, purify. The purification of garments is a metaphor (kinaya) for purifying the soul from the deeds for which one is blamed, and refining it from the states that are repugnant, because whoever is not content with impurity touching his clothing, how could he be content with impurity in his soul? It is said: "So-and-so has pure garments and clean hems and sleeves" when he is described as free from faults and the stains of character. It is also said: "So-and-so has soiled garments," and likewise "greasy garments," of the treacherous and of one whose conduct is vile. From the first usage is the poet's saying:

"He lives, unblamed for bad character, and lives, free, the one with pure garments."

From the second is his saying:

"O God, indeed Amir ibn Jahm, or one who blamed the pilgrimage, in greasy garments..."

The sayings of the majority of the early generations (salaf) revolve around this meaning in the noble verse. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatadah that he said concerning it: "Purify them from sins." It is an Arabic expression: when a man broke his word and did not keep a covenant, the Arabs would say, "So-and-so has soiled garments," and when he fulfilled it and acted rightly, they would say, "So-and-so has pure garments."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu Malik that he said concerning it: "He meant himself." Abu Malik and a group narrated from Mujahid that he said: "That is, and your deeds, so amend," and similarly from Abu Razin and al-Suddi.

He and a group, including al-Hakim who authenticated it, also narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "And your garments, purify" means: from sin. In another narration: from treachery, i.e., do not be treacherous. In a narration by a group from Ikrimah: Ibn Abbas was asked about the words of Allah the Exalted, "And your garments, purify," and he said: "Do not wear them over treachery or immorality." Then he said: "Do you not hear the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salamah:

'Indeed, by the praise of Allah, I have not worn the garment of the wicked, nor do I veil myself with treachery.'"

Similarly from al-Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr, and from al-Hasan and al-Qurtubi: that is, "And your character, beautify." They recited, to illustrate the metaphor of the self by garments, the saying of Antarah:

"I pierced with the long spear his garments; the noble is not forbidden from the spear-points."

In a narration from al-Habr (Ibn Abbas) and Ibn Jubayr, he used "garments" as a metaphor for the heart, as in the saying of Imru al-Qays:

"If indeed my disposition has displeased you, then ask my garments about your garments, and they will tell you."

It is also said that he used it as a metaphor for the body, as in the saying of Layla, when she mentioned camels that people had ridden and taken away:

"They pelted them with light garments, and we see nothing like them except the startled ostriches."

The purity of the body is also sometimes intended by this, similar to what has preceded. The relevance of these meanings to the context of the call (da'wa) is beyond dispute. It was also said that, on the basis that purifying garments is a metaphor for what has passed, this would be a command to complete the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-'ilmiyya) after the command to complete the speculative faculty and to call to it.

It was also said: it is a command to him (ﷺ) to adopt good character, which makes the warning acceptable, after his command (ﷺ), by singling out his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, with magnification (takbir), which may give the impression that he refused to lower his wing to anything other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, and that it required disregard for and indifference to those who were beneath Him, let alone the enemies of Allah, Majestic and Exalted. So its mention was to remove that misconception.

It was also said, on the interpretation of al-muddaththir as one wrapped in prophethood and perfections of the soul, the meaning being: purify the mantles of prophethood, its traces and its shining lights emanating from the niche of your essence, from what defiles them of rancor, impatience and lack of patience.

It was said that "garments" is a metaphor for women, as Allah the Exalted said: "They are garments for you" [al-Baqarah: 187]. Their purification from faults and blemishes is through admonition and discipline, as He, glorified, said: "Save yourselves and your families from a Fire" [al-Tahrim: 6].

It was also said that their purification is choosing from among them chaste believing women. It was also said that it means having intercourse with them in the vagina and not the anus, and during purity and not during menstruation; this was related by Ibn Bahr. However, the root of this saying, in my view, is far from the context. Then I saw that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) stated this explicitly.

A group, however, held that "garments" is to be taken literally, so Muhammad ibn Sirin said: "That is, wash them with water if they are najis." Something similar was narrated from Ibn Zayd, and this is the saying of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him). From here, many held that it is obligatory to wash najasa (impurity) from the garments of one who prays. And he (ﷺ) was commanded with this, according to what was narrated from Ibn Zayd, in opposition to the polytheists, for they did not keep their garments free from impurities.

It was said: a sheep's afterbirth (salaa) was thrown upon him (ﷺ), and it grieved him, so he returned to his house sorrowful and wrapped himself up. Then it was said to him: "O you wrapped up! Arise and warn" (74:1-2), and let that foolishness not prevent you from warning. "And your Lord, magnify" (74:3), from not taking vengeance on them. "And your garments, purify" (74:4) from those impurities and filth. Intending purification from impurity for prayer without taking the story into account is said to be contrary to the apparent meaning, and the sentence does not fit with what precedes it on this basis, unless "magnify" is intended to mean magnifying for prayer. Some of those who interpreted "garments" as the body allowed keeping purification in its literal sense.

It was also said: he (ﷺ) was commanded to clean himself at the time of istinja' (cleaning after relieving oneself), for the Arabs did not clean their bodies of impurity either, and many of them would urinate on their heels. Some said the command is for absolute request, for purifying what is not pure of garments is obligatory in prayer and recommended outside it.

It was said that purifying them means shortening them, and this is also a command to him (ﷺ) to abandon the blameworthy customs of the Arabs, for their custom was to lengthen garments and trail their hems out of pride and arrogance. A poet said:

"Then they went off, the fragrance of musk upon them, covering the earth with the fringes of their waist-wrappers."

In a hadith: "The lower garment of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins, and there is no fault for him in what lies between that and the ankles, but what is below that is in the Fire."

The use of purification for shortening is a metaphor, because shortening is necessarily associated with it, for lengthening them often leads to trailing their hems over filth. Some people made shortening, after intending it from purification, a metaphor for the absence of arrogance and self-conceit. That would be a command to him (ﷺ) to humility and to persistence in abandoning trailing the hems of arrogance and self-conceit, after his command to reserve greatness and majesty for Him, the Exalted, in speech and belief. As if it were said: "And your Lord, magnify" while you are not arrogant, so that the command to warn may be fulfilled for you. Some who hold that combining the literal and the metaphorical is permissible took purification in both its literal sense and its metaphorical sense, namely shortening. The reaching of such an intention is easy for one who does not hold combining them to be permissible.

It was also permitted that by purification is meant the removal of whatever is considered filthy in general, whether najis or other filthy but pure things, such as dirt. Then this would be a command to him (ﷺ) to clean his garments and remove from them dirt and anything else that is considered filthy, for it is repellent and unbefitting the station of prophethood. This necessarily implies, a fortiori, cleaning the body of such things, and therefore he (ﷺ) was the cleanest of people in garments and body. It may also be said that this implies, a fortiori, the command to avoid verbal and practical repellent conduct, such as obscenity, harshness and roughness, and so on. So do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 5:

﴿And abandon the abomination (ruzz)﴾. Al-Qutabi said: (al-ruzz) means the punishment, and its root meaning is agitation (idtirab). It has been used in place of its cause, which leads to it, namely the sins. So it is as if it were said: abandon the sins and disobediences that lead to punishment. Or the speech is by way of an elided genitive, meaning: the causes of the ruzz. Or it is metonymy in the attribution, as has been said. Similar to this is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas: (al-ruzz) is wrath (al-sukht). Al-Hasan explained (al-ruzz) as disobedience, and al-nakh' as sin, and this is an explanation of the intended meaning. Since the one addressed with this command is the Prophet ﷺ, and he is free of that, it falls under the category of: "It is you I mean, but listen, O my neighbour" (iyyaka a'ni wa-asma'i). Or the intended meaning is persistence and steadfastness in abandoning that. It has also been said that ruzz is the name of two idols, Isaf and Na'ila, and it has been said that it is a general name for idols; this was narrated from Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Zuhri, and the speech is as you have just heard. It has also been said that (al-ruzz) is a name for the ugly and loathsome thing, and "and abandon the abomination" is a comprehensive statement on noble character, as if it were said: abandon harshness, foolishness, and everything that is considered ugly, and do not adopt the characteristics of these polytheists. In light of this, it may be that this is a command to purify the inner self, following the command to purify the outer self in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾.

Most readers recited "al-rijz" with a kasra on the ra', and this is the dialect of Quraysh. According to a group, the meanings of the kasra and the damma are one. Según Mujahid, the one with damma means the idol and the one with kasra means the punishment. It has also been said that the one with kasra means shortcomings and wickedness, while the one with damma means Isaf and Na'ila. In Kitab al-Khalil, "al-rujz" with a damma on the ra' is the worship of idols, and with a kasra it is punishment. From the speech of the masters, i.e., the world, so leave it. This is based on the view that by ruzz is meant the idol, and the world is among the greatest idols whose love stands between the servant and his Master, and its worshippers are more numerous than its worshippers, for it is worshipped in churches, synagogues, monasteries, mosques and elsewhere. Or ruzz is meant as the ugly and loathsome, and the world, to the knower, is in the utmost ugliness and filthiness.

From the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honour his face, it is related that he said: "The world is more worthless than the carcass of a dead pig over which a dog urinated in the hand of a leper."

And al-Shafi'i said:

"It is nothing but a rotting carcass, over which are dogs whose only concern is to pull at it.
So if you avoid it, you will be at peace with its people, but if you pull at it, its dogs will contend with you."

It is said: everything that distracts from Allah, mighty and majestic, is ruzz, and it is obligatory for the seeker of Allah, exalted is He, to abandon it, for by this abandonment one attains union, and by this severance connection is achieved. Among the greatest distractions from Allah, exalted is He, is the self (al-nafs), and for this reason it has been said: that is, oppose your self. The speech in all of this falls under the category of "It is you I mean." Or the aim in it is persistence, and the garments are as previously mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 6:

﴿And do not bestow, seeking to receive more﴾. That is, do not give to one seeking more (*mustakthir*), meaning one who seeks much, from the person to whom you give. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. It is a prohibition against *istighzar* (seeking abundance in return), which is to give something while hoping to receive from the recipient more than what was given. This is permissible. From this is the report narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah as a statement (*mawquf*) of Shurayh: "The one who seeks more in return is rewarded for his gift." Otherwise, according to the Shafi'is, the prohibition is for prohibition (*tahrim*), and it is one of the particularities of the Prophet (ﷺ), because God Most High chose for him, peace and blessings be upon him, the most perfect attributes and the most noble character, so it was impermissible for him to give in exchange for more. It has also been said that it is a prohibition of disapproval (*tanzih*) for everyone. Or the meaning is: do not give while seeing what you give as much, so the *sin* here is for finding (*wijdan*) and not for seeking (*talab*), as in the first, apparent reading. The prohibition against this is because it is a kind of self-admiration, and it contains hidden stinginess. And from al-Hasan and al-Rabi':

Do not ﴿bestow﴾ with your good deeds upon God Most High, seeing them as many, meaning regarding them as abundant, so that they become diminished in the sight of God, Mighty and Majestic. Some of the masters counted the regarding of good deeds as abundant to be: seeing them as good deeds, not fearing their rejection, and being heedless that they come from Him, Most High, in reality.

From Ibn Zayd: Do not bestow with what God Most High has given you of prophethood and the Qur'an, seeking with it, meaning seeking much reward from people. From Mujahid: Do not weaken in your work, seeking abundance in your obedience, so that you become weak (*famtunn*), from their saying *habl manin*, meaning a weak rope. This meaning is implied by what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: meaning, do not say, "I have called them but they have not accepted from me," rather return and call them.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *tastakthir* with a sukun on the *ra'*, and it was explained as *jazm* (apocopation), with the verb being a substitute (*badal*) for *tamnun*, which is in the jussive form after the prohibitive *la*. It is as if it were said: "Do not bestow; do not seek more," because it is in the nature of one who bestows to regard what he gives as much and to count it significant. This is a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). It has also been said that it is a *badal kull min kull* (total substitution) on the basis of the claim of identity.

And in *al-Kashshaf*, the substitution from *tamnun* is on the basis that *al-mann* is counting what one has given, not the giving itself. There is a subtle point in this, because seeking more is the precursor of *mann*; it is as if it were said: "Do not seek more, let alone bestow." It was also permitted that the sukun be a true pause (*sukun waqf*), or that the connected reading be treated as a pause, or a sukun of lightening, on the basis that *thir* is likened to *'adud*, so the *ra'* between the *tha'* and the *waw* of *wa-li-rabbika* is made sukun as the *dad* was. But this is not the right view. In this case the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

Al-Hasan and al-A'mash also read *tastakthira* with a fatha, on the basis of an implied *an* (that), like their saying *murhu yahfirha* (tell him to dig it), meaning *an yahfirha* (that he dig it). And the poet's line:

Unquestionably, O you who rebuke me, saying "Attend the battle," and that I witness pleasures, will you grant me immortality?

In one narration, *ahdara* (attend) is in the accusative. Ibn Mas'ud read *an tastakthira* with *an* made explicit, so *al-mann* means giving, and the sentence is understood as expressing purpose: "Do not give in order that you seek much," meaning, seeking much from the one to whom you give. And for your Lord, be patient (﴿ولِرَبِّكَ فاصْبِرْ﴾). It has been said: "Patient over the harm of the polytheists." It has also been said: "Patient in performing the obligations (al-fara'id)."

Ibn Zayd said: "Patient in fighting the red and the black." This is far-fetched, since there was no fighting (jihad) at the time this was revealed.

It is reported from al-Nakha'i: "Patient over your giving (ʿaṭiyyatika)." It is as though he connected it to what came before and made it patience in giving without seeking to increase one's gifts.

The preferred view, as Jār Allāh (al-Zamakhsharī) said, is that it is a command to the act itself, and the meaning is to aim at His direction and side, exalted and majestic is He. So the word patience (al-ṣabr) is used in its unrestricted sense, and because the object (al-mutaʿallaq) is not specified, it includes, as a general term (al-ʿamm), every thing one is patient in and every thing one is patient against. Patience over the harm of the polytheists is meant as one individual instance of the general term, not as the only thing intended.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Patience in the Qur'an has three aspects: patience in performing the obligations, which has three hundred degrees; patience in refraining from what Allah has forbidden, which has six hundred degrees; and patience at calamities at the first shock, which has nine hundred degrees. This is because it is most difficult for the soul, and one cannot attain it except (illā) through greater certainty (yaqīn)."

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I ask You for the certainty by which You make the calamities of this world easy for me."

They also mentioned that patience, considered in terms of its ruling (ḥukm), has four categories: an obligatory (farḍ) kind, such as patience in refraining from what is prohibited and patience in performing what is required; a recommended (nafl) kind, such as patience in refraining from what is disliked and patience in performing what is sunnah; a disliked (makrūh) kind, such as patience in not performing what is sunnah and patience in doing what is disliked; and a forbidden (ḥarām) kind, such as patience toward one whose sanctity is targeted by a prohibited act, and refraining from confronting him while one is able to. And there is more to say on this in its proper place. The praiseworthy legislated patience has virtues that cannot be counted. It is enough for this His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [Az-Zumar: 10].

And His saying (ﷺ): "Allah, exalted is He, said: When I direct a calamity toward one of My servants in his body, his wealth, or his child, and he then meets that with beautiful patience, I am too shy before him on the Day of Resurrection to set up a scale for him or to spread out a register for him."

﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ﴾ means "when it is blown" (nuqira: "was blown") ﴿فِي النّاقُورِ﴾, that is, into the trumpet (al-sur). *Al-naqur* is on the pattern *fa'ul* from *al-naqr* in the sense of producing a sound. Its root meaning is striking, which is its cause, and from it comes *minqar al-ta'ir* (the bird's beak), because the bird strikes with it. Because of this causal relation, the word was used figuratively for the cause, and this became common, so that it is meant to refer to blowing, since blowing is a kind of striking. The *fa'* (ف) here indicates causation, as if it were said: "Be patient with their harm, for before them is a terrible day, on which they will encounter the consequence of their harm, and you will encounter the consequence of your patience with it."

The governing element (*al-'amil*) of *idha* (إذا) is what is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿فَذَلِكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ ﴿عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("That, on that day, is a difficult day for the disbelievers"). The meaning is: when it is blown in the trumpet, the matter becomes difficult for the disbelievers. The *fa'* here is for the apodosis (*al-jaza'*, the consequent clause). *Dhalika* (ذَلِكَ) is a reference to the time of the blowing, which is understood from ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ﴾, and the sense of distance in it, despite the closeness of the reference in wording, is to indicate that its position in terror and dreadfulness is high. Its place in the grammar is the nominative, as a subject (*mubtada'*).

﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ ("on that day") is said to be a substitute (*badal*) for it, built on the vowel *fatha* because it is attached to a non-declinable word. The predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾, as if it were said: "So the day of the blowing is a difficult day." It is also permitted for ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ to be a stable adverbial complement (*zarf mustaqarr*) of ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾, that is, a qualifier of it. When it preceded it, it became a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of it. The one who permitted this, according to what is in *al-Kashshaf*, is that the meaning is: "That, at the time of the blowing, is the occurrence of a difficult day, because the Day of Resurrection comes and occurs at the moment it is blown in the trumpet. It is like the time of spring, the festival occurs in it," meaning the occurrence of the festival in it, and the substance of that is "that occurrence is the occurrence of a day, etc." From what has been mentioned, the objection that is suspected, concerning the fronting of a complement of the verbal noun (*ma'mul al-masdar*) or of what is in its relative clause over the verbal noun, is refuted. Making the adverb of the occurrence (*zarf al-wuqu'*) or the adverb of *'asir* as implied, and stating the expression "occurrence of," is an exposition of the meaning and an escape from making a time an adverb of a time, by returning it to the event. So reflect on this. The apparent method of *al-Kashshaf* is to prefer this view, and likewise the statement of the author of *al-Kashf*, since he established it in the most complete manner and claimed that what preceded was forced. Yes, he, may God have mercy on him, also permitted that ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ may be the complement of what the apodosis indicates, as if it were said: "When it is blown in the trumpet, the matter becomes difficult for the disbelievers on that day." Whichever is the case, ﴿عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ is related to ﴿عَسِيرٌ﴾. It has also been said that it is related to an implied element, which is a qualifier of *'asir* or a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun within it.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted its attachment to ﴿يَسِيرٍ﴾ in His words, exalted is He: ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ ("not easy"). This is what the statement of Qatada implies. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it should not be permitted, because it involves fronting a complement of the genitive noun (*al-mudaf ilayhi*) over the construct noun (*al-mudaf*), which is prohibited according to the correct view. Some have permitted it with *ghayr* by analogy with *la*, so one says: "I am not pleased with Zayd" (*ana bi-Zayd ghayru radin*). Al-Hawfi claimed that *idha* is connected to *inzar* (warning) and the *fa'* is superfluous, and he meant that it is an object of *andhir* (warn), as if it were said: "Arise and warn them at the time of the blowing in the trumpet." His words, exalted is He, ﴿فَذَلِكَ﴾ and so on, form a new independent clause in the position of causal explanation, and it is as you see. Abu al-Baqa' permitted an interpretation of the verse according to the view of al-Akhfash, by making *idha* a subject (*mubtada'*) with the predicate ﴿فَذَلِكَ﴾, the *fa'* being superfluous, and making ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ an adverbial complement of *dhalika*. I do not think you doubt that this is the statement of al-Akhfash.

Some eminent scholars said that *dhalika* is a subject, and it is a reference to the verbal noun, that is, "that blowing," and it is the governing element of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾, and ﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ﴾ is the predicate of the subject, with an implied genitive construct, meaning: "that blowing, in that day, is the blowing of a day." There is in this a strain and a departure from the apparent sense, while the difficulty of the day is not the intended benefit upon it. The apparent context shows that the intended benefit is something else. The scholar al-Tibi considered this verse to be of the type in which the condition and the consequent are identical, like the saying: "Whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, then his emigration is to God and His Messenger." He made the reference to be to the time of the blowing, and said: "With the repetition, there is an indication of alerting to a great matter and a grave affair." There is something to examine in this. The benefit of His words, glorified is He, ﴿غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ﴾ ("not easy"), meaning not light, after His words, exalted is He, ﴿عَسِيرٌ﴾ ("difficult"), is to emphasize its difficulty for the disbelievers. It prevents it from being difficult for them in one respect but not another, which would imply that it is easy for the believers. As if it were said: "Difficult for the disbelievers, not easy for them, just as it is easy for their opposites, the believers." Thus there is in it a combination of threatening the disbelievers and increasing their rage, and giving glad tidings to the believers and consoling them. This does not depend on attaching ﴿عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ to ﴿يَسِيرٍ﴾; indeed the matter is more evident with it, as is not hidden. Then, even with this, the heart of the believer is not free from fear.

Ibn Sa'id and al-Hakim reported from Bihz ibn Hakim, who said: "Zurara ibn Awfa led us in prayer, and he recited *al-Muddaththir*, and when he reached ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾, he fell down dead, and I was among those who carried him."

Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'How can I be at ease, when the one who holds the trumpet has put the horn to his mouth and bent his brow, listening for when he will be commanded?' They said: 'How should we say it, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'Say: "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs," and in God we put our trust.'"

It has been disputed whether the time intended by this is the day of the first blast or the day of the second blast. It has been preferred that it is the day of the second blast, because its difficulty is specific to the disbelievers. As for the time of the first blast, its ruling, which is the swooning, includes the righteous and the wicked. According to the well-known view, it is specific to those who are alive at the time the blast occurs.

Ibn Sa'id and al-Hakim reported from Bihz ibn Hakim, who said: "Zurara ibn Awfa led us in prayer, and he recited *al-Muddaththir*, and when he reached ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾, he fell down dead, and I was among those who carried him."

Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When ﴿فَإذا نُقِرَ في النّاقُورِ﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'How can I be at ease, when the one who holds the trumpet has put the horn to his mouth and bent his brow, listening for when he will be commanded?' They said: 'How should we say it, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'Say: "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs," and in God we put our trust.'"

It has been disputed whether the time intended by this is the day of the first blast or the day of the second blast. It has been preferred that it is the day of the second blast, because its difficulty is specific to the disbelievers. As for the time of the first blast, its ruling, which is the swooning, includes the righteous and the wicked. According to the well-known view, it is specific to those who are alive at the time the blast occurs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 11:

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, as has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative governed by (adhamm) or similar, for al-Walid was nicknamed among his people "the Solitary" (al-Wahid), so God, exalted is He, mocked him with it and with his nickname; or He turned it away from the purpose for which they aimed, namely praising him and extolling him, toward dispraising and blaming him. From Qatadah: six thousand dinars. It was also said: nine thousand dinars.

From Sufyan al-Thawri there are two reports: four thousand dinars, and a million dinars.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 14:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 15:

﴿Then he desires that I should give him more.﴾ Over what I have bestowed upon him. This is an expression of disbelief and disapproval of his greed and eagerness, either because he is in complete wealth, with no addition possible beyond what he has been given in abundance and plenty, or because it is incompatible with his condition of ingratitude for blessings and his obstinate opposition to the Bestower.

It is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri) and others that he used to say: "If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me." The use of ﴿thumma﴾ (then) to express astonishment (istib'ad) is common. It has been said that this is other than the sequential gradation (al-tafawut al-rutbi); rather, considering a thing remote is unsuitable for what it is joined to, as when you say: "You wrong me, then you hope for my kindness."

This is because the moral distance (al-bu'd al-ma'nawi) is treated as if it were a temporal distance (al-bu'd al-zamani).

﴿Kalla﴾ ("No!"): a rebuke and reproof to him, cutting off his empty greed and his hopes, which will be disappointed. His statement, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our signs﴾, is a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a sentence introduced to explain what came before). It is as if it were said: why was he rebuked for seeking more, and what is the reason he is not deserving of it? So it was said: he was defiant toward the signs of the Bestower, which are the proofs of His oneness, or the Qur'anic verses, when he said about them what he said. Defiance is suited to removal and prevents any increase. Muqatil said: After the revelation of this verse, al-Walid continued to lose from his wealth and his children until he perished. ﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: I will cover him with a difficult ascent, a steep path. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ It is either an explanation (ta'lil) for the threat and his deserving it, or a clarification of his obstinacy towards His signs, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus it is an explanatory clause (jumla mufassira) for that, having no place in i'rab (grammatical case analysis), and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 19:**

﴿Destroyed be he, how he planned!﴾ This is an expression of wonder at his planning and at his success in it, in hitting the target that Quraysh had aimed at. It is similar to ﴿May God destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30; al-Munafiqun: 4]. Or it is a praise of him, in mockery, like the saying "May God destroy him, how brave he is!" Or it is a report of what they repeated as a curse when they heard his foolish words. The Arabs say "May God kill him, how brave he is," and "May God shame him, how perceptive he is," meaning that he has reached the level at which he deserves to be envied, and his envier invokes this against him. As for what has been said about the first meaning, though the aspect differs, it has been narrated that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he recited the Qur'an to him, and it seemed that he was softened by it. This reached Abu Jahl, who said: "O uncle, your people want to gather wealth for you and give it to you, for you came to Muhammad to obtain something from what he has." He said: "Quraysh know that I am among the richest of them in wealth." He said: "Then say something about him that will reach your people, that you deny it and that you hate it." He said: "And what should I say? By God, there is no man among you who knows poetry better than I do, neither its rajaz nor its qasidah, nor the poetry of the jinn. By God, what he says does not resemble any of this. By God, his words have a sweetness, and upon them is a radiance, and their top is fruitful and their bottom is abundant. It rises and is not surpassed, and it shatters what is beneath it." He said: "Your people will not be pleased with you until you say something about him." He said: "Leave me until I think." When he had thought, he said: "This is nothing but magic that is learned." So they were amazed by that.

And Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) said: "When the verses ﴿Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ up to His saying ﴿the final return﴾ [Ghafir: 1-3] were revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Prophet stood in the mosque while al-Walid was near him, listening to his recitation. When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, noticed his listening, he repeated the recitation. Al-Walid went to the assembly of his people, Banu Makhzum, and said: 'By God, I have just heard from Muhammad a speech that is neither the speech of men nor the speech of jinn. Indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a radiance; its top is fruitful and its bottom is abundant. It rises and is not surpassed.' Quraysh said: 'By God, al-Walid has become a Sabian! By God, all of Quraysh will become Sabians!' Abu Jahl said: 'I will take care of him for you.' He sat down beside him, grieved, and spoke to him in a way that angered him. He stood up and came to them and said: 'You claim that Muhammad is a madman; have you seen him choking? You say he is a soothsayer; have you ever seen him foretell? You claim he is a poet; have you seen him engaged in poetry? You claim he is a liar; have you ever tested him with any lie?' They said, to all of that: 'No, by God.' Then they said: 'So what is he?' He thought, then said: 'He is nothing but a sorcerer. Have you not seen that he separates a man from his wife, his child, and his clients? And what he says is nothing but magic that he has transmitted from Musaylimah and the people of Babylon.' The assembly erupted with joy, and they dispersed, impressed by his words and amazed at them."

﴿Then he was killed, how he calculated﴾ is a repetition for emphasis (mubalaghah), as is customary after *u'jiba* (he was amazed) when expressing extreme admiration. The conjunction *thumma* (then) indicates a difference in rank (*tafawut al-rutbah*), and the second phrase is more emphatic than the first. It is as if it were said: "He was killed with some kind of killing? No, he was killed with its severest and most severe form." For this reason it was permissible for the conjunction to appear here, even though it is a repetition (*ta'kid*). Similar to this is what is found in the verse:

*And I have no wrong against them that I know of, except that I said: "O tree of Sarhah, be safe."*

*Be safe, be safe, then be safe, then be safe: three greetings, even if you do not speak.*

The praise expressed in the admiration through its wording indicates the utmost mockery of him and of the one who rejoiced at the result of his thinking. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said in *Ghurrat al-Tanzil*: When al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah was asked about the Prophet ﷺ, he calculated what he had brought of the Qur'an and said: "If we say he is a poet, the Arabs will call us liars when they compare what he has brought with poetry." By this calculation he intended to deny the Messenger ﷺ through a kind of deception (*ihtiyal*). [p. 124] Therefore every calculation deserved punishment from God Most High, which is like killing in its destruction of him. So the first (*Qutila*) refers to his calculation about poetry, meaning: he is destroyed with the destruction of one who is killed, however he calculated. And God's words ﴿then he was killed, how he calculated﴾ refer to his other calculation, for he also calculated. He said: If we claim that what he brought is the speech of soothsayers, the Arabs will call us liars when they see this speech differs from the speech of the soothsayers. Then in his calculation about the speech of the soothsayers, he deserves punishment which is like killing in destroying him. Thus this came for this, and there is no repetition in the reiteration.

The first view is what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) took, and he considered the supplication (*du'a'*) to be a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*). Al-Tibi said about it: it is not of the commonly known type of parenthetical insertion, which is for embellishing speech and affirming it, because the *fa'* (so) prevents that. Rather it is from the speech of another, and the *fa'* occurred within his words, so it was inserted between two connected statements by way of narration (*hikayah*). Then he said: this is far-fetched, and he only took this path because he made the two supplications part of another's speech. But if they are made part of God Most High's speech, as mockery (*istihza'*) as he mentioned, or as a curse upon him, as al-Raghib went, and as al-Wahidi's exegesis is according to what he said, and it is reported from Sahib al-Nazm (the author of *al-Nazm*): ﴿So he was killed how﴾, meaning: he was tormented and cursed, ﴿how he calculated﴾, as one says, "I will certainly strike him, however he behaves," meaning: in whatever state he was from him, so that the actions are all harmonious and ordered according to the gradations in sequence and delay in time and rank, as the context requires, and the arrangement came in accordance with the familiar pattern of revelation, and so on to the end of what he said. What preceded is farther in meaning, and the parenthetical insertion is of the commonly known type, and it emphasizes what the speech was directed toward in the best emphasis. The *fa'* is not an obstacle, according to what Jar Allah and others stated explicitly, and he counted among the parenthetical insertions accompanied by it the verse ﴿So ask the people of remembrance﴾ [al-Nahl: 43; al-Anbiya': 7], and among them the verse:

*Know, for the knowledge of a man benefits him, that everything that has been decreed will surely come.*

He verified that it is in reality a conclusion placed between the parts of the speech out of concern for its matter, so it served the function of a parenthetical insertion and is counted as one. The parenthetical insertion is between God Most High's words ﴿Indeed he thought and calculated﴾.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then he looked﴾. The particle "then" (thumma) here and in what follows is a conjunction ('atf) retaining its lexical meaning (al-ma'na al-wad'i), namely temporal sequence with an interval: that is, "then he reflected upon the matter of the Qur'an once and then again." ﴿Then he frowned﴾: he contracted his face when he found no grounds for criticism in it and his stratagems were exhausted, and he did not know what to say. It was also said: he looked at the faces of the people, then he frowned. It was also said: he looked at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then he frowned at his face, upon him be prayers and peace. ﴿And he scowled﴾, that is, he displayed frowning before its time and out of its proper occasion. Al-busr is haste in something, as in the expression "basara al-rajul li-hajatin" (the man hastened for a need he sought outside its proper time). "Basara al-fahl al-naqah" means the stallion mounted the she-camel before she sought it. "Ma' busr" means water taken from its pool before it has settled. It was also said that an unripe fruit that is picked before ripening is called busr, and from this it is said that when a fruit has not ripened it "basara." Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) explained it here in this sense. Some explained it as the most intense frowning, from "basara" when one contracts the space between the eyebrows out of aversion to something and the face turns dark from it. It is also used in the sense of frowning, and from it is the verse of Tawba:

"Her aversion from me has troubled me, which I have seen,
and her turning away from my need, and her sullenness."

And the saying of Sa'd, when he had embraced Islam: "My mother estranged me, and she would meet me once with cheerfulness and once with sullenness (al-busr)." In that case the mention of "basara" serves as an emphasis for "⁠ʿabasa." Perhaps this is what the one who said "it follows him" (ittiba' lahu) intended. The people of Yemen (Ahl al-Yamin) say "basara al-markab" and "absara" when a ship stopped. I have not seen anyone who permits that this meaning is intended here, even if remotely, and I have some reservation about whether this usage is established as sound Arabic.
