Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 26:

﴿Soon I shall cast him into Saqar.﴾ It is a substitute (badal) for ﴿I shall overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾, etc., a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because Saqar includes hardships and a mountain of fire. The attribute that follows does not contradict the substitution, on the basis that the meaning of the mountain is like what is in the hadith. Abu Hayyan said: It appears that they are two sentences, each of which follows on the path of threatening the disobedience that precedes each of them. So he threatened, for his being stubborn toward the signs of Allah the Exalted, with overwhelming by a steep ascent, and for his saying that the Qur'an is magic that is transmitted, with being burned in Saqar. And in this there is a discussion that is not hidden from one who has comprehensive knowledge of what preceded.

And what will make you know what Saqar is? That is: what thing informed you of what Saqar is? Here "ma" in the first instance is a subject (mubtada'), and "adraka" (what made you know) is its predicate, while the second "ma" is a predicate because it conveys what is intended by way of awe and terror. "Saqar" is a subject (mubtada'), meaning: what is it in its description? For "ma" may be used to ask about a description, although it is more common for it to be used to ask about a name and a reality.

The Most High's words, ﴿It spares not, nor leaves [anything]﴾, are an explanation of its description and state. So the clause is either explanatory or a fresh sentence, with no need to make it the predicate of an omitted subject. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to ﴿Saqar﴾, with the governing element being the sense of magnification: "How great is Saqar and how terrible its affair, in that it ﴿spares not﴾," and so on. But this is not the right view. That is, it does not spare anything cast into it without destroying it, and once it has destroyed it, why would it leave it destroyed so that it must be restored?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿It spares not﴾ means: when it seizes them, it leaves none of them, and when they are changed into a new creation, it does not leave off returning them to the first torment. Something similar is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, with the addition: "and for everything there is a respite and weariness, except Jahannam." It has also been said: ﴿It spares not﴾ anything upon which it lays hold, nor does it leave it from destruction; rather, everything cast into it is certainly destroyed. Al-Suddi said: it leaves them no flesh and spares no bone, but this is weaker than what came before.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 29:

﴿Scorching the human skin.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Abu Razin and the majority said: that is, it alters the complexions and blackens the skins. In some narrations transmitted from some of them, the addition "burning" (muhraqah) appears. The general meaning of ﴿lawwahah﴾ is from "lawahat-hu al-shams" (lawahah, the sun has tanned and blackened his outer surface and extremities). He said:

"She says: What has tanned you, O traveller, O daughter of my paternal uncle? The noonday heats have tanned me."

Al-bashar is the plural of bashrah (bashrah: the outer layer of the skin). Some reports state that it strikes the skin with a blast that leaves it blacker than the night. It was objected that it is not correct to describe it as blackening the outer skins while Allah, glorified is He, says ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾, which is explicit about burning. It was answered that at first contact it blackens, then it burns and destroys, or that the first describes its state with one who enters it, and this is its state with one who draws near to it. You know that if it is said that it is not fitting to describe it as blackening the outer skins after describing it as ﴿leaving nothing and sparing nothing﴾, this answer is not fitting. It may then be answered that the intent is to mention its terrifying, dreadful attributes without intending a progression from the terrible to the more terrible, and that being ﴿lawwahah﴾ is one of its attributes, perhaps considered with respect to the first contact. It was also said that destruction is meant, and that mentioning it contains the horror it contains, because blackening the skins, apart from the pain it causes, is a disfigurement of creation and a mutilation of the person; so it falls under the category of tatmim (completing the description). Regarding whether blackening the skins entails destruction there is hesitation, and even if it is said so, consider this carefully. He also permitted, on the interpretation of ﴿lawwahah﴾ mentioned, that al-bashar be a collective noun meaning "people", and the meaning returns to what preceded.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Kaysan and al-Asamm said: ﴿lawwahah﴾ is an intensive form from laha (to appear, become visible), and al-bashar means "people"; that is, it appears to people because of its greatness and dread, as the Exalted said: ﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾. It has been reported that it appears to them from a distance of five hundred years. The nominative ﴿lawwahah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is lawwahah." ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi, Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿lawwahatan﴾ in the accusative, as a restrictive (ikhtisas) accusative for the sake of awe, meaning "I single out" or "I mean." He also permitted that it be an emphatic circumstantial accusative (hal mu'akkadah) from the pronoun in ﴿tubqi﴾ or ﴿tadhar﴾, on the basis of the claim of entailment, and that it be a circumstantial accusative from ﴿saqar﴾, with the governing element being what has passed.

[Page 125]

﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ The apparent meaning is that they are angels. Do you not see how the Arabs, who were eloquent, understood it in this sense? It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the verse ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said to the Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! I hear that the son of Abu Kabsha tells you that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, and you are a multitude. Would every ten of you be unable to overpower one man from among them?" Abu al-Ashadd ibn Usayd ibn Kaladah al-Jumahi, who was very strong, said to him: "I will suffice you against seventeen; then you suffice me against two." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels﴾, meaning: We have not made them men of your kind whom you could overpower. And God, glorified is He, revealed concerning Abu Jahl: ﴿Woe to you, and woe again! Woe to you, and woe again!﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:34–35].

The apparent meaning is that by "the companions of the Fire" are meant the nineteen. In that case, the explicit noun is placed in the position of a pronoun. It seems that this was done because this explicit wording indicates that they are the ones who manage its affairs and who carry out the punishment of its inhabitants, something the pronoun does not convey. This also indicates that by Saqar is meant the Fire in general, not a particular stratum of it.

The majority hold that by them are meant the chiefs (nuqaba'). So the meaning of their being ﴿over it﴾ is that they take charge of its affairs, and to them belongs the command of its guardians (zabaniyah). Otherwise, it has been reported: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand bridles, and with each bridle seventy thousand angels dragging it."

Some have held that the omitted specifier (tamyiz) is ṣinf (a kind), and it has been said that it is ṣaff (a row). The original would be: over it nineteen ﴿kinds﴾, or over it nineteen ﴿rows﴾. This view is weakened by what preceded in the report of the scholar (al-habr), and likewise by God's saying: ﴿And We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. For what is immediately understood is that their temptation (of the disbelievers) lies in their independence and in their considering it far-fetched that nineteen should be in charge of punishing the majority of the two groups (humans and jinn), and in their mocking it. But with the specifier ṣinf or ṣaff, this would not hold.

Many have said, in explaining why they were made angels: so that they would be different from the kind of those who are punished, so that they would not be softened toward them and would not incline to them; and because they are the strongest of creation, the most upright in the right of God, and the most zealous for His sake, glorified is He, and the most fierce in might.

And in the hadith: "As if their eyes were lightning, and as if their voices were trumpets (siyasi), dragging their hair. For them is the strength of the two weighty ones (humans and jinn). One of them will come with a nation of people, driving them by his neck, with a mountain, until he throws them into the Fire, and then throws the mountain upon them."

It is not far-fetched that the tanwin (nunation) in the word implies the greatness of their affair. As for God's saying: ﴿And We have not made their number…﴾ to the end, according to what some of the eminent scholars have chosen, the meaning is: We have not made the number of the companions of the Fire except the number that required the disbelievers' trial through independence and mockery, which is nineteen. So the original would be: ﴿And We have not made their number except﴾ nineteen. Thus He expressed the effect, which is the trial of those who disbelieved, by the cause, which is specifically the nineteen, since the reason for their temptation is known. It has also been said: ﴿except as a trial for those who are over it, nineteen﴾, as an indication that the effect here is inseparable from its cause, since they are mutually entailed, as if they were one thing, and the name of one of them is used to denote the other. The meaning of "making their number" in an absolute sense is "the specific number", namely to report that their number is such-and-such, since "making" does not relate to the number itself but to what is counted. So the meaning is: He informed us that their number is nineteen and no other.

﴿So that those who were given the Book may be certain﴾, that is, so that they may acquire certainty of his prophethood, peace be upon him, and that the Qur'an is true, because of the agreement of those mentioned in the Qur'an with this number, and it is so in the two Books (the Torah and the Gospel). This differs from the creation of the angels in a specific number, because that is an act of bringing into being. It is not valid, as some of the verifiers have said, to make their creation in this attribute the cause of the aforementioned certainty, because it is only for agreement. Some have strained to correct this by saying that the creation is a cause of the report, and the report is a cause of certainty, so it is a remote cause of it, and a thing may be attributed to its remote cause as it is to its proximate cause. But, as he said, this is not appropriate. The interpretation was only needed by expressing the effect through the cause, and the statement does not remain on its apparent sense, because making (ja'l) belongs to the subject-predicate structure, so what follows from it follows by the relation of one of the two objects to the other, as in your saying: "I made the silver a ring for adornment with it," and likewise: "I made the silver only a ring for such-and-such." There is no sense in arranging certainty and what follows it upon making their number a trial for the disbelievers, nor does their being tempted by the specific number have any role in that. What has a role is the number itself, that is, the number considered as the specific number, and the report of it as you have heard. This is not a distortion of the Book of God, exalted is He, nor is it based on defending a false doctrine, as one might suppose. Some have strained to make the causal relation apparent by what the ear dislikes, so we will not blacken the pages with it.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan): ﴿so that they may be certain﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and it relates to ﴿We made﴾, not to ﴿trial﴾. So the trial is not an effect of certainty; rather, the effect is the making of the number as a cause of the trial.

In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir): it is permissible for the phrase ﴿so that they may be certain﴾ to refer to what precedes the exception, that is: We made their number a cause of the trial of the disbelievers and of the certainty of the believers. Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned two possibilities in this. The second is what we have already put forward, which some of the eminent scholars have chosen. The first is that the complete sentence is: ﴿And We have not made their number except as a trial﴾ for the disbelievers, and except ﴿so that those who were given the Book may be certain﴾. He said: This is like saying: "I did such-and-such for your honor and to belittle your enemy," so the conjunctive waw may sometimes be mentioned in this position and sometimes omitted. Some have said that it is connected to an omitted element, that is: We did that so that they may be certain, etc. But all of these, as you see, are unconvincing.

Some have taken ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ to mean the people of both Books, which is the view of a group. Others have said that it refers specifically to the Jews. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th have reported from al-Bara' that a group of Jews asked one of the Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, about the guardians of Hell. He replied: "God and His Messenger know best." He then came and informed the Prophet, peace be upon him, and at that very moment this verse was revealed to him: ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾

al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh have reported from Jabir, who said: Some Jews said to some Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Does your Prophet know the number of the guardians of Hell?" They informed the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and he said: "It is thus and thus," once saying ten and once saying nine.

From this it is inferred that the verse is Medinan, because the Jews were present there. This inference is weak, because the question came from a Companion, and perhaps he was traveling and met a Jew wherever he was. Also, at that time there was no barrier to some Jews coming toward Mecca the Honored. Moreover, the two reports do not necessitate restricting the relative pronoun to the Jews, as is evident. Therefore it is better to keep the definiteness generic, and the relative pronoun to include both groups: that is, ﴿so that they may be certain﴾, namely the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, ﴿and that those who believe may increase in faith﴾, that is, their faith increases in quality by what they have seen of the People of the Book's submission and their affirmation that it is so; or in quantity, by adding this belief to their belief in everything else that was revealed.

﴿And that those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt﴾: this is an emphasis on what came before it, namely certainty and the increase of faith, and a negation of whatever doubt a person who is certain might be subject to, due to heedlessness of some premises, or the arising of what was imagined to be a contradiction at first glance. Because this additional element is present, it is permissible to conjoin it to the emphasized clause with the conjunctive waw, since the two are different in general. The believers were not included in the same string as the People of the Book in the negation of doubt, since He did not say "and they may not doubt." This is to alert us to the difference between the two negations in their state: the absence of doubt among the People of the Book accompanies what contradicts it, which is denial; while among the believers it accompanies what faith requires. And how great is the difference between them! It has also been said: the reason He did not say "and they may not doubt," but rather "and that… may not doubt," is to specify the emphasis on the two matters, because the pronoun in that might return to the believers only. The expression of the believers by the active participle after mentioning them by the relative pronoun and the verbal clause, which indicates occurrence, is to announce their steadfastness in faith after their increase and firm establishment in it.

﴿And that those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is, doubt or hypocrisy, which makes it the case that the whole surah is Meccan, since hypocrisy arose only in Medina; this is a prediction of unseen matters that would occur after the Hijrah. ﴿And the disbelievers﴾, those who persist in denial, ﴿say: What did God intend by this as a parable?﴾, that is: What thing did God, exalted is He, intend by this number, which is strange in the manner of a parable? According to the first reading, "mādhā" is treated as a single interrogative word in the accusative position, governed by "arāda" (intended). According to the second reading, it is composed of the interrogative "mā" as subject and "dhā" as relative pronoun as predicate, and the sentence after it is its relative clause, with its returning pronoun omitted. "Mathalan" is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz) or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in His saying: ﴿This is the she-camel of God, a sign for you﴾ [al-A'raf 7:73; Hud 11:64].

The apparent meaning is that the words of this sentence are part of the reported speech, and by the demonstrative they meant belittling, and their aim was to deny in the strongest way that this came from God, mighty and majestic is He, not a real question about its wisdom, nor a criticism of its containing it, although they acknowledged that the reports of it came from Him, exalted is He. It is permissible that "God intended" is part of the reporting, and they said "what was intended?" or something similar. It has also been said that "mathal" may have its other meaning, which is that which is compared with its source, in that they may have considered it a parable made up because it was strange, and attributed it to Him, mighty and majestic, in mockery and derision.

The mention of this causal clause on its own, even though it is part of the trial of them, is said to be to indicate its independence in its outrageousness. In the Shihabi glosses (Hashiyat al-Shihab al-Khafaji) it is said: the particle "li-" is repeated in it only to distinguish between the two causes, since the first refers to guidance intended in itself, and this one refers to misguidance intended incidentally, arising from the bad conduct of the misguided. Explaining God's acts by wisdoms and benefits is permissible according to the verifiers. It is also permitted for this particle, and likewise the first one, to be for consequence (al-'aqibah).

﴿Thus God misguides whom He wills﴾: "dhālika" refers to what precedes it, namely the meaning of misguidance and guidance. Its grammatical position is originally the accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). The original sense is: God misguides whom He wills, ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, misguidance and guidance being of the same kind as what has been mentioned of misguidance and guidance. So the verbal noun is omitted and its adjective is put in its place, and then it is placed before the verb to convey restriction, so the structure becomes like "such misguidance and such guidance": ﴿God misguides﴾, exalted is He, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to misguide, by turning his choice, according to his bad disposition, toward the side of error when he witnesses the signs of God, exalted is He, which speak of guidance.

﴿And guides whom He wills﴾ to guidance, by turning his choice, according to his good disposition, when witnessing those same signs, toward the side of guidance; not misguidance and guidance of a lesser degree than those two. It is also permissible for the demonstrative to refer to what follows, as in His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143], according to what has been verified in its proper place.

﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord﴾: "junud" is the plural of "jund," which became famous for the army, by analogy with "jund" in the sense of hard ground, that is, land that is rough and contains stones. It is said of every gathering as well. That is: none knows the multitudes of His creation, exalted is He, of which the angels mentioned are a part, according to what they are, ﴿except He﴾, mighty and majestic is He, since no one has any way to enumerate the possible things.

[Page 129]

...the comprehension of its realities and attributes, even in summary, let alone knowing the details of its conditions, such as its quantity, its manner and its relation [to other things]. ("This") is a rebuttal of their mockery. "Over it are nineteen" [means] the guardians are nineteen, because of their ignorance of the wisdom behind that.

Muqatil said: it is an answer to the saying of Abu Jahl: "Does the Lord of Muhammad have helpers other than nineteen?" The summary of this is that, since he (Abu Jahl) belittled the helpers, he was answered that they cannot be counted for their multitude; the ones entrusted with the Fire are only these specified ones. It does not mean that no one knows the might of the strength of the angels, ("except") He. This is contrary to al-Tibi, for the wording does not clearly indicate this meaning.

There is disagreement about the greater part of the hosts of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said they are the angels, based on the report: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a place the size of a foot in it where there is not an angel standing, bowing or prostrating." ("Except") ...

And in some reports: "The created beings of the land are a tenth of the created beings of the sea, and the total is a tenth of the created beings of the air, and the total is a tenth of the angels of the lowest heaven, and the total is a tenth of the angels of the second heaven, and so on up to the seventh heaven, and the total is a tenth of the angels of the Kursi, and the total is a tenth of the angels surrounding the Throne, and the total is a very small amount in comparison with what ("except") Allah knows." It has also been said: the total is a very small amount in comparison with the sovereign angels (al-muhayminin), of whom none knows that Allah the Exalted created anyone other than Himself; and the total is a very small amount in comparison with what He, glorified be He, knows of His creatures.

From al-Awza'i, who said: Musa, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, who is with You in the heaven?" He said: "My angels." He said: "How many are they?" He said: "Twelve tribes." He said: "How many is each tribe?" He said: "The number of the dust."

The soundness of this report is questionable, and even if it is sound, its beginning belongs to the ambiguous (mutashabih) texts. I do not affirm that any one category is the majority. "None knows the hosts of your Lord ("except") He." No explicit text has been established for me on this matter. However, it is most likely in assumption that the majority are the angels, peace be upon them. This verse and similar verses and reports encourage the view that there may be, among the heavenly bodies, hosts from the hosts of Allah the Exalted whose realities and conditions none knows ("except") He, Mighty and Majestic. The domain of the kingdom of Allah, Majestic in His majesty, is far too great to be encompassed by the bounds of limitation, or for the bird of thought to reach its center. ("How, then?") Far from it, even if powers and times were exhausted.

This is what was said about the specifier of this number, namely nineteen. It has been said that the difference among human souls in reflection and action is due to the twelve animal faculties: that is, the five inner senses, the five outer senses, and the motivating faculty such as the irascible and the appetitive, and the moving faculty. These are twelve. And the natural faculties are seven, of which three are served (makhduma): the nutritive, the growth-producing and the generative; and four are serving (khadima): the digestive, the attractive, the expulsive and the retentive. This, though based on philosophy, is hardly complete, as is not hidden from one who has studied their books.

It has also been said: Hell has seven levels, six of which are for classes of unbelievers, and each class is punished, by abandoning belief, affirmation and action, with kinds of punishment suited to them. So multiplying six by three yields eighteen, and for each kind there is an angel or a category that is in charge of it. And one (level) is for the sinners of this community, who are punished there by abandoning action with a kind suited to them, and an angel or a category is in charge of it. With this the nineteen are complete. Six of them were specified for categories of unbelievers, and one for categories of this community. The punishment of unbelievers was not placed in five of them, so two remain for believers: one for the people of major sins and the other for the people of minor sins; or one for the sinners among them and the other for sinful women. Since the Fire was prepared primarily and essentially for unbelievers, it was appropriate that they should fill it entirely and be distributed over all its places as far as possible. But since His, glorified be He, will was attached to punishing the sinners of this community in it, one of its levels was separated for them.

It has also been said: the hours are twenty-four, five of which are devoted to prayer, so no guardians were created corresponding to them, because of the blessing of prayer, which includes whoever does not pray. So nineteen remain. It has also been said: Hell has seven levels, six of which are for classes of unbelievers. And for the attention to their punishment and its continuance, it was appropriate that three should be in charge of it: one in the middle and two at the two ends. So these are eighteen. And one of them is for the sinful believers, and it was appropriate for the matter of their punishment that one should be in charge of it. With this the nineteen are complete.

It has also been said that number is of two kinds: few, which is from one to nine, and many, which is from ten onward ("except") that which has no end. So he combined the end of the few with the beginning of the many. It has also been said other than this. What most scholars incline to is that this is among what no one knows the wisdom of with certainty ("except") Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is like the ambiguous (mutashabih) texts: one believes in it and entrusts its knowledge to Allah the Exalted. All that has been mentioned, apart from what can be relied upon, is not hidden from one who directs even a little attention to it. And Allah the Exalted is the Guide to the right path, and He bestows favor on whom He wills; He knows, and there is no doubt or uncertainty with Him.

Abu Ja'far and Talhah ibn Sulayman recited ﴿تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ﴾ with the ʿayn sukun (ʿashar), and this is a dialect form of it, disliking the succession of vowels in what is like a single noun. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Qutb and Ibrahim ibn Qattah recited "tusʿata" with a damma on the tāʾ, and this is a vowel of construction (binaʾ) that they moved to from the fatha, to avoid the succession of five fathas. It should not be supposed that it is a vowel of inflection (iʿrab), otherwise ʿashara would have been inflected.

Anas also recited "tusʿata" with a damma and "aʿshara" with a fatha. The author of al-Lawami says: it is possible that he made ʿashara into aʿshur, then treated it as tisʿata ʿashara. It is also reported from him: "tusʿata" and "ʿushara" with a damma and the conversion of the hamza into a pure waw for lightness, and the tāʾ in both is pronounced with a damma of construction, for what you have heard just now. From Sulayman ibn Qattah, the brother of Ibrahim, it is reported that he recited "tisʿata aʿshurin" with a damma on the tāʾ as an inflectional damma, and with the genitive and its annexation to aʿshur, and its genitive case, unnunated. This, as the author of al-Lawami says, is the plural of ʿashara, and he explicitly stated that the angels according to this plural reading, whether inflected or indeclinable, are ninety angels. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the plural of ʿashir, like yamin and ayman.

It is reported from him that he said: that is, nine angels, each one of whom is an ʿashir (companion), so they, with their followers, are ninety, and ʿashir has the meaning of ʿashr (ten). Thus it indicates that the chiefs are nine. This was objected to on the grounds that its indication of this meaning is not clear. For this reason Ibn Jinni said: there is no basis for that reading, ("except") that it means "tisʿu aʿshurin," the plural of ʿashir, and they are the friends. So let it be reviewed.

[Page 130]

("And what it is") — that is, Saqar, as the speech of Mujahid implies — ﴿إلا ذكرى للبشر﴾ "except a reminder to mankind," that is, a reminder for them. The conjunction has been said to be with His saying, ﴿سأصليه سقر﴾ "I will burn him in Saqar," and ﴿وما جعلنا أصحاب النار﴾ "and We did not make the companions of the Fire," up to here as a parenthetical clause. Its rationale is that when it was said ﴿عليها تسعة عشر﴾ "over it are nineteen," as an increase in the terror of the matter of Hell, it was followed by what confirms their strength, their domination, and their distinction by severity from all other creatures. ﴿[Then]﴾ by what confirms the quantity; and what confirms the confirmed is also confirmed.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the verses speaking of the conditions of Saqar. It has also been said that it refers to the number of its guardians, and the reminder and admonition in it is from the aspect that among the creation of Allah the Exalted there is what is of the utmost greatness, so that a few of them can punish and destroy countless numbers, as evidence that He, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be measured by His true measure, nor can His greatness be described, nor can thoughts reach the sanctuary of His majesty.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the hosts, and it has been said that it refers to the fire of this world. This is the weakest of the sayings, and the strongest of them, as has been said, is what preceded.

Between "al-bashar" here and "al-bashar" in what came before, namely His saying, ﴿لواحة للبشر﴾ "scorching to mankind," according to the interpretation of the majority, there is a complete verbal and orthographic paronomasia (tajnis tamm), and few notice it.

It is not far-fetched that the tanwin (nunation) in the word implies the greatness of their affair. As for God's saying: ﴿And We have not made their number…﴾ to the end, according to what some of the eminent scholars have chosen, the meaning is: We have not made the number of the companions of the Fire except the number that required the disbelievers' trial through independence and mockery, which is nineteen. So the original would be: ﴿And We have not made their number except﴾ nineteen. Thus He expressed the effect, which is the trial of those who disbelieved, by the cause, which is specifically the nineteen, since the reason for their temptation is known. It has also been said: ﴿except as a trial for those who are over it, nineteen﴾, as an indication that the effect here is inseparable from its cause, since they are mutually entailed, as if they were one thing, and the name of one of them is used to denote the other. The meaning of "making their number" in an absolute sense is "the specific number", namely to report that their number is such-and-such, since "making" does not relate to the number itself but to what is counted. So the meaning is: He informed us that their number is nineteen and no other.

﴿So that those who were given the Book may be certain﴾, that is, so that they may acquire certainty of his prophethood, peace be upon him, and that the Qur'an is true, because of the agreement of those mentioned in the Qur'an with this number, and it is so in the two Books (the Torah and the Gospel). This differs from the creation of the angels in a specific number, because that is an act of bringing into being. It is not valid, as some of the verifiers have said, to make their creation in this attribute the cause of the aforementioned certainty, because it is only for agreement. Some have strained to correct this by saying that the creation is a cause of the report, and the report is a cause of certainty, so it is a remote cause of it, and a thing may be attributed to its remote cause as it is to its proximate cause. But, as he said, this is not appropriate. The interpretation was only needed by expressing the effect through the cause, and the statement does not remain on its apparent sense, because making (ja'l) belongs to the subject-predicate structure, so what follows from it follows by the relation of one of the two objects to the other, as in your saying: "I made the silver a ring for adornment with it," and likewise: "I made the silver only a ring for such-and-such." There is no sense in arranging certainty and what follows it upon making their number a trial for the disbelievers, nor does their being tempted by the specific number have any role in that. What has a role is the number itself, that is, the number considered as the specific number, and the report of it as you have heard. This is not a distortion of the Book of God, exalted is He, nor is it based on defending a false doctrine, as one might suppose. Some have strained to make the causal relation apparent by what the ear dislikes, so we will not blacken the pages with it.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan): ﴿so that they may be certain﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and it relates to ﴿We made﴾, not to ﴿trial﴾. So the trial is not an effect of certainty; rather, the effect is the making of the number as a cause of the trial.

In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir): it is permissible for the phrase ﴿so that they may be certain﴾ to refer to what precedes the exception, that is: We made their number a cause of the trial of the disbelievers and of the certainty of the believers. Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned two possibilities in this. The second is what we have already put forward, which some of the eminent scholars have chosen. The first is that the complete sentence is: ﴿And We have not made their number except as a trial﴾ for the disbelievers, and except ﴿so that those who were given the Book may be certain﴾. He said: This is like saying: "I did such-and-such for your honor and to belittle your enemy," so the conjunctive waw may sometimes be mentioned in this position and sometimes omitted. Some have said that it is connected to an omitted element, that is: We did that so that they may be certain, etc. But all of these, as you see, are unconvincing.

Some have taken ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ to mean the people of both Books, which is the view of a group. Others have said that it refers specifically to the Jews. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th have reported from al-Bara' that a group of Jews asked one of the Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, about the guardians of Hell. He replied: "God and His Messenger know best." He then came and informed the Prophet, peace be upon him, and at that very moment this verse was revealed to him: ﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾

al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh have reported from Jabir, who said: Some Jews said to some Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Does your Prophet know the number of the guardians of Hell?" They informed the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and he said: "It is thus and thus," once saying ten and once saying nine.

From this it is inferred that the verse is Medinan, because the Jews were present there. This inference is weak, because the question came from a Companion, and perhaps he was traveling and met a Jew wherever he was. Also, at that time there was no barrier to some Jews coming toward Mecca the Honored. Moreover, the two reports do not necessitate restricting the relative pronoun to the Jews, as is evident. Therefore it is better to keep the definiteness generic, and the relative pronoun to include both groups: that is, ﴿so that they may be certain﴾, namely the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, ﴿and that those who believe may increase in faith﴾, that is, their faith increases in quality by what they have seen of the People of the Book's submission and their affirmation that it is so; or in quantity, by adding this belief to their belief in everything else that was revealed.

﴿And that those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt﴾: this is an emphasis on what came before it, namely certainty and the increase of faith, and a negation of whatever doubt a person who is certain might be subject to, due to heedlessness of some premises, or the arising of what was imagined to be a contradiction at first glance. Because this additional element is present, it is permissible to conjoin it to the emphasized clause with the conjunctive waw, since the two are different in general. The believers were not included in the same string as the People of the Book in the negation of doubt, since He did not say "and they may not doubt." This is to alert us to the difference between the two negations in their state: the absence of doubt among the People of the Book accompanies what contradicts it, which is denial; while among the believers it accompanies what faith requires. And how great is the difference between them! It has also been said: the reason He did not say "and they may not doubt," but rather "and that… may not doubt," is to specify the emphasis on the two matters, because the pronoun in that might return to the believers only. The expression of the believers by the active participle after mentioning them by the relative pronoun and the verbal clause, which indicates occurrence, is to announce their steadfastness in faith after their increase and firm establishment in it.

﴿And that those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is, doubt or hypocrisy, which makes it the case that the whole surah is Meccan, since hypocrisy arose only in Medina; this is a prediction of unseen matters that would occur after the Hijrah. ﴿And the disbelievers﴾, those who persist in denial, ﴿say: What did God intend by this as a parable?﴾, that is: What thing did God, exalted is He, intend by this number, which is strange in the manner of a parable? According to the first reading, "mādhā" is treated as a single interrogative word in the accusative position, governed by "arāda" (intended). According to the second reading, it is composed of the interrogative "mā" as subject and "dhā" as relative pronoun as predicate, and the sentence after it is its relative clause, with its returning pronoun omitted. "Mathalan" is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz) or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in His saying: ﴿This is the she-camel of God, a sign for you﴾ [al-A'raf 7:73; Hud 11:64].

The apparent meaning is that the words of this sentence are part of the reported speech, and by the demonstrative they meant belittling, and their aim was to deny in the strongest way that this came from God, mighty and majestic is He, not a real question about its wisdom, nor a criticism of its containing it, although they acknowledged that the reports of it came from Him, exalted is He. It is permissible that "God intended" is part of the reporting, and they said "what was intended?" or something similar. It has also been said that "mathal" may have its other meaning, which is that which is compared with its source, in that they may have considered it a parable made up because it was strange, and attributed it to Him, mighty and majestic, in mockery and derision.

The mention of this causal clause on its own, even though it is part of the trial of them, is said to be to indicate its independence in its outrageousness. In the Shihabi glosses (Hashiyat al-Shihab al-Khafaji) it is said: the particle "li-" is repeated in it only to distinguish between the two causes, since the first refers to guidance intended in itself, and this one refers to misguidance intended incidentally, arising from the bad conduct of the misguided. Explaining God's acts by wisdoms and benefits is permissible according to the verifiers. It is also permitted for this particle, and likewise the first one, to be for consequence (al-'aqibah).

﴿Thus God misguides whom He wills﴾: "dhālika" refers to what precedes it, namely the meaning of misguidance and guidance. Its grammatical position is originally the accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). The original sense is: God misguides whom He wills, ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, misguidance and guidance being of the same kind as what has been mentioned of misguidance and guidance. So the verbal noun is omitted and its adjective is put in its place, and then it is placed before the verb to convey restriction, so the structure becomes like "such misguidance and such guidance": ﴿God misguides﴾, exalted is He, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to misguide, by turning his choice, according to his bad disposition, toward the side of error when he witnesses the signs of God, exalted is He, which speak of guidance.

﴿And guides whom He wills﴾ to guidance, by turning his choice, according to his good disposition, when witnessing those same signs, toward the side of guidance; not misguidance and guidance of a lesser degree than those two. It is also permissible for the demonstrative to refer to what follows, as in His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143], according to what has been verified in its proper place.

﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord﴾: "junud" is the plural of "jund," which became famous for the army, by analogy with "jund" in the sense of hard ground, that is, land that is rough and contains stones. It is said of every gathering as well. That is: none knows the multitudes of His creation, exalted is He, of which the angels mentioned are a part, according to what they are, ﴿except He﴾, mighty and majestic is He, since no one has any way to enumerate the possible things.

[Page 129]

...the comprehension of its realities and attributes, even in summary, let alone knowing the details of its conditions, such as its quantity, its manner and its relation [to other things]. ("This") is a rebuttal of their mockery. "Over it are nineteen" [means] the guardians are nineteen, because of their ignorance of the wisdom behind that.

Muqatil said: it is an answer to the saying of Abu Jahl: "Does the Lord of Muhammad have helpers other than nineteen?" The summary of this is that, since he (Abu Jahl) belittled the helpers, he was answered that they cannot be counted for their multitude; the ones entrusted with the Fire are only these specified ones. It does not mean that no one knows the might of the strength of the angels, ("except") He. This is contrary to al-Tibi, for the wording does not clearly indicate this meaning.

There is disagreement about the greater part of the hosts of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said they are the angels, based on the report: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a place the size of a foot in it where there is not an angel standing, bowing or prostrating." ("Except") ...

And in some reports: "The created beings of the land are a tenth of the created beings of the sea, and the total is a tenth of the created beings of the air, and the total is a tenth of the angels of the lowest heaven, and the total is a tenth of the angels of the second heaven, and so on up to the seventh heaven, and the total is a tenth of the angels of the Kursi, and the total is a tenth of the angels surrounding the Throne, and the total is a very small amount in comparison with what ("except") Allah knows." It has also been said: the total is a very small amount in comparison with the sovereign angels (al-muhayminin), of whom none knows that Allah the Exalted created anyone other than Himself; and the total is a very small amount in comparison with what He, glorified be He, knows of His creatures.

From al-Awza'i, who said: Musa, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, who is with You in the heaven?" He said: "My angels." He said: "How many are they?" He said: "Twelve tribes." He said: "How many is each tribe?" He said: "The number of the dust."

The soundness of this report is questionable, and even if it is sound, its beginning belongs to the ambiguous (mutashabih) texts. I do not affirm that any one category is the majority. "None knows the hosts of your Lord ("except") He." No explicit text has been established for me on this matter. However, it is most likely in assumption that the majority are the angels, peace be upon them. This verse and similar verses and reports encourage the view that there may be, among the heavenly bodies, hosts from the hosts of Allah the Exalted whose realities and conditions none knows ("except") He, Mighty and Majestic. The domain of the kingdom of Allah, Majestic in His majesty, is far too great to be encompassed by the bounds of limitation, or for the bird of thought to reach its center. ("How, then?") Far from it, even if powers and times were exhausted.

This is what was said about the specifier of this number, namely nineteen. It has been said that the difference among human souls in reflection and action is due to the twelve animal faculties: that is, the five inner senses, the five outer senses, and the motivating faculty such as the irascible and the appetitive, and the moving faculty. These are twelve. And the natural faculties are seven, of which three are served (makhduma): the nutritive, the growth-producing and the generative; and four are serving (khadima): the digestive, the attractive, the expulsive and the retentive. This, though based on philosophy, is hardly complete, as is not hidden from one who has studied their books.

It has also been said: Hell has seven levels, six of which are for classes of unbelievers, and each class is punished, by abandoning belief, affirmation and action, with kinds of punishment suited to them. So multiplying six by three yields eighteen, and for each kind there is an angel or a category that is in charge of it. And one (level) is for the sinners of this community, who are punished there by abandoning action with a kind suited to them, and an angel or a category is in charge of it. With this the nineteen are complete. Six of them were specified for categories of unbelievers, and one for categories of this community. The punishment of unbelievers was not placed in five of them, so two remain for believers: one for the people of major sins and the other for the people of minor sins; or one for the sinners among them and the other for sinful women. Since the Fire was prepared primarily and essentially for unbelievers, it was appropriate that they should fill it entirely and be distributed over all its places as far as possible. But since His, glorified be He, will was attached to punishing the sinners of this community in it, one of its levels was separated for them.

It has also been said: the hours are twenty-four, five of which are devoted to prayer, so no guardians were created corresponding to them, because of the blessing of prayer, which includes whoever does not pray. So nineteen remain. It has also been said: Hell has seven levels, six of which are for classes of unbelievers. And for the attention to their punishment and its continuance, it was appropriate that three should be in charge of it: one in the middle and two at the two ends. So these are eighteen. And one of them is for the sinful believers, and it was appropriate for the matter of their punishment that one should be in charge of it. With this the nineteen are complete.

It has also been said that number is of two kinds: few, which is from one to nine, and many, which is from ten onward ("except") that which has no end. So he combined the end of the few with the beginning of the many. It has also been said other than this. What most scholars incline to is that this is among what no one knows the wisdom of with certainty ("except") Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is like the ambiguous (mutashabih) texts: one believes in it and entrusts its knowledge to Allah the Exalted. All that has been mentioned, apart from what can be relied upon, is not hidden from one who directs even a little attention to it. And Allah the Exalted is the Guide to the right path, and He bestows favor on whom He wills; He knows, and there is no doubt or uncertainty with Him.

Abu Ja'far and Talhah ibn Sulayman recited ﴿تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ﴾ with the ʿayn sukun (ʿashar), and this is a dialect form of it, disliking the succession of vowels in what is like a single noun. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Qutb and Ibrahim ibn Qattah recited "tusʿata" with a damma on the tāʾ, and this is a vowel of construction (binaʾ) that they moved to from the fatha, to avoid the succession of five fathas. It should not be supposed that it is a vowel of inflection (iʿrab), otherwise ʿashara would have been inflected.

Anas also recited "tusʿata" with a damma and "aʿshara" with a fatha. The author of al-Lawami says: it is possible that he made ʿashara into aʿshur, then treated it as tisʿata ʿashara. It is also reported from him: "tusʿata" and "ʿushara" with a damma and the conversion of the hamza into a pure waw for lightness, and the tāʾ in both is pronounced with a damma of construction, for what you have heard just now. From Sulayman ibn Qattah, the brother of Ibrahim, it is reported that he recited "tisʿata aʿshurin" with a damma on the tāʾ as an inflectional damma, and with the genitive and its annexation to aʿshur, and its genitive case, unnunated. This, as the author of al-Lawami says, is the plural of ʿashara, and he explicitly stated that the angels according to this plural reading, whether inflected or indeclinable, are ninety angels. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the plural of ʿashir, like yamin and ayman.

It is reported from him that he said: that is, nine angels, each one of whom is an ʿashir (companion), so they, with their followers, are ninety, and ʿashir has the meaning of ʿashr (ten). Thus it indicates that the chiefs are nine. This was objected to on the grounds that its indication of this meaning is not clear. For this reason Ibn Jinni said: there is no basis for that reading, ("except") that it means "tisʿu aʿshurin," the plural of ʿashir, and they are the friends. So let it be reviewed.

[Page 130]

("And what it is") — that is, Saqar, as the speech of Mujahid implies — ﴿إلا ذكرى للبشر﴾ "except a reminder to mankind," that is, a reminder for them. The conjunction has been said to be with His saying, ﴿سأصليه سقر﴾ "I will burn him in Saqar," and ﴿وما جعلنا أصحاب النار﴾ "and We did not make the companions of the Fire," up to here as a parenthetical clause. Its rationale is that when it was said ﴿عليها تسعة عشر﴾ "over it are nineteen," as an increase in the terror of the matter of Hell, it was followed by what confirms their strength, their domination, and their distinction by severity from all other creatures. ﴿[Then]﴾ by what confirms the quantity; and what confirms the confirmed is also confirmed.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the verses speaking of the conditions of Saqar. It has also been said that it refers to the number of its guardians, and the reminder and admonition in it is from the aspect that among the creation of Allah the Exalted there is what is of the utmost greatness, so that a few of them can punish and destroy countless numbers, as evidence that He, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be measured by His true measure, nor can His greatness be described, nor can thoughts reach the sanctuary of His majesty.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the hosts, and it has been said that it refers to the fire of this world. This is the weakest of the sayings, and the strongest of them, as has been said, is what preceded.

Between "al-bashar" here and "al-bashar" in what came before, namely His saying, ﴿لواحة للبشر﴾ "scorching to mankind," according to the interpretation of the majority, there is a complete verbal and orthographic paronomasia (tajnis tamm), and few notice it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verses 32–33:

﴿Kallā﴾ is a rebuke (radʿ) to those who deny it (i.e., the verses). It is also said to be a warning (zajr) against the claim of Abu Jahl and his companions that they could resist the guardians of Hell (khazanat Jahannam). It is also said: a rebuke against mockery of the specified number (of the guardians). Al-Farra' said: it is a connective particle (silah) for the oath, and some have estimated it as ḥaqqan (truly), while others have estimated it as alā, the particle of opening (al-istiftāḥiyyah, "verily").

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a denial (inkār) after He, glory be to Him, had made it a reminder (dhikrā), that they should have a reminder. Abu Hayyan criticised him, saying that it is not permissible with regard to Him, exalted is He, to inform that it is a reminder for mankind and then deny that it is a reminder for them. It has been answered that there is no contradiction, because the meaning of its being a reminder is that its nature is to remind everyone; and whoever does not take heed, due to the dominance of wretchedness over him, is not counted among mankind and is not regarded for his failure to take heed, just as the sweetness of honey is not harmed by its being bitter in the mouth of one whose temperament is disordered and who needs treatment. The goodness of pausing at kallā, and its lack of goodness here, is known from considering the intended meaning of it.

Some have stated this explicitly, saying: if it is connected to the preceding speech, it is good to pause upon it; and if it is connected to the following speech, that is not good. That is, just as it is in the sense of alā, the particle of opening, the pause is then complete at "for mankind," and it begins anew with ﴿Kallā, by the moon﴾ ﴿and by the night when it turns back﴾, i.e., when it departs (wallā).

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Abu al-Zinad, Qatadah, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Hasan, Talhah, the two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyan), the two sons (al-Ibnan), and Abu Bakr read ﴿idhā﴾ as a temporal adverb of future time, and ﴿dabara﴾ with a fatḥah on the dāl. It has the meaning of ﴿adbara﴾ (the augmented form), as in qabala and aqbala, though the common form is the augmented one (al-mazīd).

The use of the triliteral form here is for the sake of matching the majority of the verse-endings (fawāṣil). It has also been said that dabara is from dubur al-layl, "the back of the night," meaning the day follows it (khalafahu). The use of the past tense with idhā, which is for the future, serves to affirm (taḥqīq) the event. It is also permissible to say that it (idhā) turns it (the verb) into the future.

Abu Razin, Abu Raja', al-Aʿmash, Matar, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd, and a narration from al-Hasan, Ibn Yaʿmur, al-Sulami, and Talhah read ﴿idhā﴾ with an alif (إذا), and ﴿adbara﴾ with the hamzah. Likewise it is in the codices of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and Ubayy (ibn Kaʿb), and this is more fitting to His saying, exalted is He.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verses 34–35]**

﴿And by the dawn when it brightens﴾, i.e., it shone and became clear, according to the reading of the majority. Ibn al-Sumayfi' and Isa ibn al-Fadl read «سَفَرَ» (safara) as a triliteral verb, and interpreted it as the removal of darkness from its face. ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest (calamities)﴾ is the answer to the oath. It is also permissible that ﴿Nay﴾ be a rebuke to one who denies that it is one of the greatest, because of what is known of the emphatic «إنّ» (inna) and the «لام» (lam of emphasis) being used in speech that rejects a stubborn denier. This is the reason given for ﴿Nay﴾. The oath is parenthetical, for emphasis, and has no answer, or its answer is understood and indicated by ﴿Nay﴾. There is some obscurity in this explanation, so reflect on it.

The pronoun in ﴿indeed it﴾ refers to Saqar. «الكُبَرِ» (al-kubar) is the plural of «الكُبْرى» (al-kubra), with the feminine alif treated like its feminine ta'. Just as «فُعْلَةٌ» is pluralized as «فُعَلٌ», «فُعْلى» is pluralized in the same way. Parallels include «السَّوافِي» as the plural of «السّافِياءِ» and «القَواصِعُ» as the plural of «القاصِعاءِ». Others maintained that it is an active participle (ism fa'il) in the sense of *mundhirah* (warning). Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 38:

﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ — mar'hunatun ('indallahi ta'ala bi-kasbiha), i.e., it is held as a pledge with God, the Exalted, on account of what it has earned. Al-rahina (الرَّهِينَةُ) is a verbal noun (masdar) with the meaning of al-rahn (the pledge/pawning), like al-shatimah (الشَّتِيمَةُ) with the meaning of al-shatm (insult). It is not an adjective; otherwise it would have been said rahin (رَهِينٌ), because fa'il in the sense of maf'ul does not take the taa' marbuta, and its masculine and feminine forms are the same. From this is the saying of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, when his father had been killed and seven blood-wealth payments (diyat) were offered to him, and he refused to accept them:

Does he who is in the valley of Na'f Nu'ayk-ib [seem far?]
A pledge of a grave of earth and gravel...

I remind [them] of the sparing of those who struck me, ***
and my sparing is that I strive, not growing weary.

Rahin (رَهِينٍ) was chosen over rahinah with its balance against al-yamin (the oath) and because it needs no interpretation, since the masdar here is more emphatic (abligh), and so it is more fitting to the context; therefore one should not turn to the verbal correspondence in it. It has been said that the taa' in ﴿رَهِينَةٌ﴾ is for intensification (li-al-mubalagha). Abu Hayyan preferred that it is among those words in which nominalization has come to predominate (ghalaba 'alayhi al-ismiyyah), like al-nati hah (النَّطِيحَةُ), even though the original is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul; this is also a valid view. He also claimed that the feminine form in the verse is according to the meaning of al-nafs (the soul).

﴿Except the companions of the right hand﴾. They are the sincere believers (al-Muslimun al-mukhlisun), as said by al-Hasan, Ibn Kaysan and al-Dahhak, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas: they are "freeing their necks (fakkun riqabahum) because of the good deeds they did, just as the mortgagor (al-rahin) redeems his pledge by paying the debt."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and a group related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that they are the children of the Muslims.

They also related it from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Some reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the angels, for they are not held in pledge by the debts of obligations, like children. This was criticized on the grounds that applying the word "soul" (nafs) to an angel is not well known, and that angels are also not described as "earning" (kasb). The majority of scholars hold the interpretation mentioned above. Some said they are those for whom the best reward (al-husna) from Allah has preceded. Others said they are those who were at the right of Adam, peace be upon him, on the Day of the Covenant (yawm al-mithaq). Others said they are those who will be given their books in their right hands. There is no contradiction between these sayings, as is clear. The exception (istithna') according to what was mentioned earlier is connected (muttasil), and likewise these sayings. As for the view of the Amir, may Allah ennoble his face, and what was reported from his cousin, Abu Hayyan said: it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'). It was also said that both connection and disconnection are permissible, based on whether kasb means any action or only what is an obligation (taklif). So do not overlook this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verses 40–42:

﴿In gardens﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the tanwin (nunation) of *jannat* is for magnification. The sentence is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) that serves as an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, namely the exception of the companions of the right (*ashab al-yamin*). It is as if it were said: "What is their state?" And it was said: "They are in gardens whose reality cannot be grasped and whose description cannot be attained." It is also permitted that the adverbial phrase be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating either to *ashab al-yamin* or to their pronoun in His words ﴿they will ask one another﴾. It was placed first for emphasis while observing the rhyme (*fasila*). It has also been said that it is an adverbial complement of *tasa'ul* (asking). The intended meaning of their asking is not that each of them asks the other in such a way that each is both asker and asked together. Rather, the asking proceeds from them without being directed at them. For the *tafa'ul* form (*sighat al-tafa'ul*), although it was originally coined to indicate that an action proceeds from a transitive agent and falls upon the other simultaneously, so that each one becomes both doer and object together, as in your saying *tashatama al-qawm* ("the people insulted one another," meaning each one insulted the other), it may nevertheless be stripped of the second meaning, intending only the first, with the object of the action being something else. An example is your saying: "You see him and the crescent (moon)."

Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said: When the speaker is singular, he says *da'awtuhu* ("I called him"), and when he is plural, he says *tada'aynahu* ("we called him"). Its parallel is *ramaytuhu* ("I shot at him") and *taramaynahu* ("we shot at him"), and *ra'aytu al-hilal* ("I saw the crescent") and *ta'ara'aynahu* ("we saw it"). This *tafa'ul* does not occur reciprocally from both sides. On this basis, the one asked is omitted, namely the guilty ones. The estimated reading is ﴿they will ask﴾ the guilty ones about them, that is, they will ask the guilty ones about their conditions. It was altered to what is in the sublime arrangement. It has also been said that the reading is ﴿they will ask about the guilty ones﴾, and the meaning on that reading is as follows. The omission of the one asked is because he is not the one about whom the question is asked.

As for His words ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾, it is an explanation of the asking, without any need to posit an implied speech, or it is considered to be implicitly governed by a saying, and it occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the agent of ﴿they will ask﴾. That is, they ask them, saying: "What has caused you to enter Saqar?" It has also been said that the one asked is other than the guilty, such as a group of the angels, peace be upon them. And ﴿what has brought you﴾ etc. is the narration of the speech of those asked about them. That is, when the companions of the right asked the angels about the state of the guilty, they said to them: "We asked the guilty ones about that, and we said to them: 'What has brought you into Saqar?'" to the end of the verse. It would have sufficed for them to say that their state was such and such, but he brought the answer in detail according to what they asked, so that it would be more firmly established as truth and more indicative of the reality of the matter. Thus there is omission and abridgement in the speech.

It is also permitted that the *tafa'ul* form be in its literal sense, that is, some of them ask one another about the guilty, and ﴿what has brought you﴾ is the narration of the speech of those asked about them as well. The drawback of considering it as narration is not hidden, and although conciseness is the method of the Revelation and omission is frequent in His sublime speech, that is not the preferable view. The apparent meaning is that the question is one of reproach and humiliation, for otherwise they know well what brought them into the Fire. Even if they were children, in my opinion, this is because the matter will be made clear on that day. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad and a group related from Ibn al-Zubayr that he used to recite: "They will ask about the guilty ones, O so-and-so, what has brought you into Saqar?" It is also related from ʿUmar. Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Masʿud that he recited: "O you disbelievers, what has brought you into Saqar?"

Even if they were children, in my opinion, this is because the matter will be made clear on that day. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad and a group related from Ibn al-Zubayr that he used to recite: "They will ask about the guilty ones, O so-and-so, what has brought you into Saqar?" It is also related from ʿUmar. Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Masʿud that he recited: "O you disbelievers, what has brought you into Saqar?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verses 43–44:

﴿They said﴾, that is, the criminals, answering the questioners, ﴿"We were not among those who prayed"﴾ to the obligatory prayer, ﴿"nor did we feed the needy"﴾; that is, we did not give him what it was obligatory to give him. The meaning is according to the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation.

The verse has been used as evidence that the disbelievers are addressed by the particular obligations of the acts of worship (furu' al-'ibadat), since they made their punishment due to abandoning the prayer; and if they were not addressed by them, they would not be held accountable. The detailed treatment of this question is in the books of usul (usul al-fiqh). This argument has been objected to on the grounds that there is no disagreement regarding being held accountable in the Hereafter for abandoning belief (i'tiqad), so it is possible that the meaning is "among those who believed in the prayer and its obligation," and the punishment is for abandoning belief. Also, "those who used to engage in falsehood" (al-mudilin) may be a metaphor for the believers. Also, that is part of the speech of the disbelievers, so it is possible that they lied or erred in it. It has been answered that this is a departure from the apparent meaning, which is rejected by the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿"and we did not use to feed the needy"﴾, etc.

The purpose of narrating the question and answer is warning. So if the answer were a lie or an error, there would be no benefit in mentioning it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 45:

﴿And we used to plunge into vain talk along with those who plunged.﴾ That is, we used to begin ( nashra'u) in falsehood along with those who began in it. Al-khawd (plunging) originally means beginning to enter water and passing through it, and its use for beginning falsehood is of the metonymic figure of speech (al-majaz al-mursal) or a metaphor (isti'arah), as they have established regarding the word al-mishfar (lip) and similar words. It is also reported from some scholars that it is a term predominantly used for evil, and that in the Qur'an it is mostly used in a context that censures engaging in it. By falsehood is meant whatever is not fitting in speech and action. Among this is counted, for example, relating what takes place between spouses in privacy, relating the conditions of sinners of various kinds in a manner of delight and enjoyment in them, and transmitting the wars that took place among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, for no legitimate purpose, but merely as a means to reach slander and disparagement; and speaking a word by which a man makes his companions laugh, whether the word is permissible in itself or not. Yes, speaking a forbidden word for such a purpose is falsehood upon falsehood, and other things beyond counting. The mention of ﴿with those who plunge﴾ indicates their lack of concern for falsehood and their indifference to it, as if they were saying: "We used to be unconcerned with falsehood."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 46:

﴿And we used to deny the Day of Religion﴾ That is, the Day of Recompense. They attributed it to the recompense, although that Day contains calamities and terrors without limit, because it is the most calamitous and the most terrifying of them, and because they are involved in it. The rest of the calamities have already passed, and the delay in mentioning this sin of theirs, although it is greater than all the others, is for the sake of magnifying it. It is as if they said: "And we were, after all of that, deniers of the Day of Resurrection." It also serves to show that their denial of it accompanied all their other enumerated sins, continuing until the end of their lives, as their statement indicates.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 47:

﴿Until there came to us the certainty.﴾ That is, death and its precursors, as most of the exegetes have held. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The certainty (al-yaqin), in my view, is the realization of what they used to deny, namely the return to Allah, the Exalted, and the Hereafter. The statement of the exegetes that it is death is, in my view, open to objection, because death itself is a certainty for the disbeliever while he is still alive. So they did not mean by 'certainty' anything other than (illa) the thing they used to deny while they were alive in this world, and they came to be certain of it after death." End of quote. But there is room for scrutiny in this.

Then, the apparent meaning is that the whole of what they mentioned is the cause of their entire group entering the Fire. Nothing in that contradicts the fact that among the people of the Fire there are those who had not been obligated to feed a poor person, such as the destitute poor among the disbelievers. In al-Kashshaf it is said: the statement may allow that each of them entered the Fire for the combination of all four (matters), and it may allow that some of them entered for some of them, such as that it was for merely neglecting the prayer or neglecting to feed (the poor). In this there is a subtle trace of Mu'tazilism, namely the eternal damnation of a grave sinner among the believers, such as one who abandons the prayer, in the Fire. And you know that the verse concerns the disbelievers, not those more general than them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verses 48–49:

﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them﴾. "Even if they all interceded for them" (لَوْ شَفَعُوا لَهم جَمِيعًا). The statement is on the basis of a supposition (al-farḍ), and it is well known that it belongs to the category of the line: "And you do not see the lizard (al-ḍabb) going into its hole (ينجحر)." Taking the definite article (al-ta'rīf) in الشّافِعِينَ to denote comprehensiveness (al-istighrāq, inclusion of all members of the category) is more eloquent and more suitable to the context.

The fa' (الفاء) in His words ﴿So what is wrong with them, that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ is for the sequencing (li-tartīb) of the denunciation of their turning away from the Qur'an without any cause, upon what precedes it of the factors that call for turning towards it and being admonished by it, from the evil state of those who deny (al-mukadhdhibīn). مُعْرِضِينَ is a necessary circumstantial clause (ḥāl lāzima) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase (al-jār) that occurs as the predicate (khabar) of مَا the interrogative (al-istifhāmiyya), namely لَهم, and it is the intended meaning of the statement. عَنِ is connected to it. The fronting (al-taqdīm) is for emphasis (al-'ināya) while observing the rhyme (ra'āyat al-fāṣila, the verse-ending). That is: since the state of those who deny it is as mentioned, what has happened to them that they turn away from the Qur'an, when the factors calling for turning towards it are mutually reinforcing and the motives towards belief in it are pulling them?

He also permitted that التَّذْكِرَةِ (al-tadhkira, the reminder) be understood as including the Qur'an and whatever else is comprehended by it, but what follows favours the first (interpretation). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the meaning of al-tadhkīr (admonishing), which is the origin, according to what was mentioned, for the sake of intensification (mubālagha).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 50:

Page 134
His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿As if they were startled donkeys﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "turning away" (mu'ridin), by way of interpenetration (tadakhul). "Ḥumur" is the plural of "ḥimar" (donkey), and what is meant by it, as Ibn 'Abbas said, is the wild donkey (ḥimar al-wahsh), because it is proverbial among the Arabs for its skittishness and its intense fleeing. (And "mustanfirah") is from istanfara, in the sense of nafara (to flee), like 'ajiba and ista'jaba, as has been said. The better view is that the form istaf'ala here expresses intensification, as if the donkeys, because of the intensity of their running, seek to flee from themselves, and the meaning is: likened to donkeys that are extremely fleeing.

﴿Fa-rrat min qaswarah﴾: that is, a lion. The word is of the pattern *fa'ūlah* (فَعُولَةٌ) from *al-qasr*, meaning subjugation and overpowering. Ibn Jarir, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others transmitted this from Abu Hurayrah. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from Ibn ʿAbbas as well, except that he said it is in the language of the Arabs "the lion" (al-asad), and in the language of Abyssinia *qaswarah* (﴿قَسْوَرَةٍ﴾). In another report from him: it refers to men who are archers and hunters. A similar report is transmitted from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Ibn Jubayr and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah. In another report from him, which Ibn ʿUyaynah recorded in his *Tafsir*, it means the murmur of people, that is, their voices. Also from him: the nets of hunters.

From Qatadah: the arrows. Ibn al-Aʿrabi and Thaʿlab said: *al-qaswarah* is the first part of the night, that is, they fled from the darkness of the night. The majority of the linguists hold that it is the lion. Whichever it is, they are compared, in their turning away from the Qur'an and their refusal to listen to its admonitions, and their fleeing from it, to wild donkeys which, in their flight, were startled by something that frightened them. In likening them to donkeys there is clear reproach and a debasement of their condition, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿like a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 5]. Or it is a testimony against them of foolishness and lack of intellect.

Al-Aʿmash read *ḥumrun* (حُمْرٌ) with the *mīm* sukun. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Mufaddal from ʿĀṣim read *mustanfarah* (مُسْتَنْفَرَةٌ) with a *fatḥah* on the *fāʾ*, meaning that their fright had roused them (*istanfarahā*) from the lion. The reading *farrat* (فَرَّتْ) suits the *kasrah*. On the authority of Muhammad ibn Sallam, who said: I asked Abu Sirar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, about ﴿as if they were donkeys﴾, and he said: *mustanfarah*, which a lion had driven away, and he pronounced the *fāʾ* with a *fatḥah*. I said: It is only ﴿fled from a lion﴾. He said: "Did it flee?" I said: Yes. He said: Then it is *mustanfarah* with a *kasrah* on the *fāʾ*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Nay, every man of them desires that he be given scrolls spread out﴾, is a conjunction (ʿatf) with an implied element required by the context, as if it were said: they are not content with that reminder, nor are they satisfied with it; rather, every one of them desires to be given sheets that are unrolled and read, like the letters that are exchanged among people. It is also permitted that what is meant is books that were written in the heaven and that the angels brought down, spread out upon their hands at the moment they were written, fresh and moist, not yet folded. This has a remoteness. And on both interpretations, they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "If it pleases you that we follow you, then bring each one of us a book from the heaven, its address being: from the Lord of the worlds, to so-and-so son of so-and-so, in which we are commanded to follow you." So it was revealed.

Similar to it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will not believe in your ascending until you bring down to us a book that we may read﴾ [al-Isra': 93], and His saying: ﴿Even if We had sent down to you a writing on paper, and they had touched it with their hands﴾ [al-An'am: 7], the verse. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, who said: They said, "If Muhammad is truthful, let there be in the morning under the head of each man of us a sheet in which there is acquittal and security from the Fire." It was also said: they used to say, "We have been informed that a man from the Children of Israel would wake up with his sin and its expiation written upon his head; so bring us the like of that." And this is far from the spread-out scrolls.

(Except) that what is meant by the spread-out scrolls is the writings that are apparent and manifest. Similar to it is what is related from Abu Salih, so both return to one meaning, since both share that what is spread out has not remained in its original state, and that each has a particular sheet belonging to him, either for his deliverance from sin or for a way of salvation. The relied-upon interpretation is what precedes, and it is related from al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "ṣuḥfan" with a sukun on the ḥa' and "munashsharah" with the lightened form, on the basis that anshara al-ṣuḥuf and nashara-hā are one, like anzala and nazzala. In al-Bahr (al-Muhit): what is preserved in a sheet or a garment is "nushira," lightened, triliteral. It is said of the dead: "anshara-hu Allah" and "nashara-hu"; and it is said: "anshara-hu Allah," so he "nashara," that is, He gave him life, so he came to life.

﴿Nay﴾: a rebuke against their desire for that, and a restraining of them from demanding signs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 74, verses 53–55:

﴿Nay, but they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ Therefore they turn away from the reminder, not because the giving of scrolls is impossible or because their demand is fulfilled, as they claim. Abu Haywa read "تَخافُونَ" (takhafun, "you fear") with the taa' of address, as an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them for their turning away. ﴿Innahu﴾ refers to the Qur'an, or to the reminder mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ The same applies to the pronoun that follows. And it is "dhikr" because it means the Qur'an, or it is the remembrance (dhikr).

﴿Indeed, it is a reminder﴾, and what a reminder it is! ﴿So whoever wills﴾ to remember it ﴿will remember it﴾ and, by means of it, attain the happiness of both abodes. The pause on "kalla" is as you have heard in both places, and the pause on "munashsharah" and "al-akhirah" is as well, if [the particle] is taken, as in the marginal notes, to mean "illa" (except).

﴿And they do not remember﴾, that is, merely by their own will to remember, as is understood from the apparent sense of His saying, ﴿So whoever wills, let him remember it﴾, since the will and volition of the servant have no effect on his actions. This is His saying, glorified is He, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾. It is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) taken from the most general of the causes or the most general of the states. That is: ﴿And they do not remember﴾ by any cause, or in any state, ﴿unless﴾ Allah, exalted is He, wills, or while Allah wills it. This is an explicit statement that the actions of servants occur by the will of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, either directly or through an intermediary. It is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and their interpretation of the will as the will of compulsion and coercion is a departure from the apparent sense without any compulsion or coercion.

Nafi', Sallam and Ya'qub recited ﴿tadhkuruna﴾ with the second person (ta' of address), an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), with the dhal sukun. It is also narrated from Abu Haywa, ﴿yadhdhakkaruna﴾ with the third person (ya' of absence) and the dhal shaddah. And from Abu Ja'far, ﴿tadhdhakkaruna﴾ with the upper ta' and its assimilation into the dhal.

﴿He is the One deserving of piety﴾, that is, worthy that His punishment be feared, that He be believed in and obeyed. Thus taqwa (piety) is a verbal noun of the passive form (al-mabni lil-maf'ul), meaning "that which is to be feared." ﴿And the One deserving of forgiveness﴾, worthy that He, exalted and majestic, forgive whoever believes in Him and obeys Him. Thus maghfirah (forgiveness) is a verbal noun of the active form (al-mabni lil-fa'il).

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), al-Hakim, who graded it sahih (sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others narrated from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, ﴿He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness﴾, and said: "Your Lord has said: I am worthy that I be feared, so no god is made with Me. Whoever fears Me and does not make another god with Me, then I am worthy to forgive him."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas, marfu' (traced to the Prophet, ﷺ), something close to this.

And in a hadith narrated by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, exalted is He, says: Indeed I find Myself shy before My servant who raises his hands to Me and then returns them empty without forgiveness. The angels said: Our God, He is not deserving of that. Allah, exalted is He, said: Rather, I am the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness. I call you to witness that I have forgiven him."

It seems that the sentence serves to confirm the warning and the encouragement that the preceding speech implied, as is not hidden from the one who reflects.

It is also related from some of them that when he heard His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He is the One deserving of piety and the One deserving of forgiveness﴾, he said: "O Allah, make me of the people of piety and the people of forgiveness," on the basis that the first of the second is like the second of the first, in the active form, and the second of the second is like the first of the first, in the passive form. Otherwise the supplication would not be fitting, even if one strains to make it correct. So understand. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.
